                - REBASE
                    - USAGE
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > When you run `git rebase <base-branch>`, Git performs the following steps:
                        > 
                        > 1. **Saves** your current branch's unique commits to a temporary area.
                        > 2. **Resets** your current branch to the same state as the target `<base-branch>`.
                        > 3. **Applies** your saved commits one by one on top of the new base.
                        >     
                        >     **Git +2**
                        >     
                        >     [Git](data:image/png;base64,)
                        >     
                        > 
                        > Because Git creates brand new commits (with new hashes) for your changes, the history appears as if you developed your features sequentially after the latest changes in the main branch. **GeeksforGeeks +1**
                        > 
                        > [GeeksforGeeks](data:image/png;base64,)
                        > 
                        > **Key Benefits**
                        > 
                        > - **Linear History:** Eliminates unnecessary "merge commits," making the project history much easier to read and navigate.
                        > - **Clean Pull Requests:** Standard practice in many teams is to [**rebase a feature branch**](https://docs.gitlab.com/topics/git/git_rebase/) before merging to ensure a clean, fast-forward merge into the main branch.
                        > - **Conflict Resolution:** It allows you to resolve conflicts one commit at a time rather than all at once in a massive merge.
                        >     
                        >     **about.gitlab.com +4**
                        >     
                        >     [about.gitlab.com](data:image/png;base64,)
                        >     
                    
                    > **Git rebase** is **a command used to integrate changes from one branch into another by "replaying" a sequence of commits onto a new base commit**
                    > 
            - WORKFLOW
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > ## 🔄 Workflow (Collaboration Layer)
                > 
                > > How teams use Git
                > > 
                > - Feature branching
                > - Git Flow
                > - Pull Requests (PRs)
                > - Code reviews
                > 
                > 👉 This is **real-world usage**
                > 
                > 💡 Key idea:
                > 
                > > “Git is not just local — it enables collaboration at scale.”
                > > 
            - REBASE vs MERGE
                - REBASE
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > ## 1. 🔹 Rebase (Interactive)
                > 
                > ❗ *Never rebase shared/public branches because it rewrites history.*
                > 
                > You covered rebase, but missing:
                > 
                > ```
                > git rebase-i HEAD~3
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Used for:
                > 
                > - squash commits
                > - edit commit messages
                > - clean history
                > 
                > 💡 Interviewers LOVE this
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Rebase
                > 
                > > **Rebase moves (replays) commits from one branch onto another, rewriting history.**
                > > 
                > 
                > ```
                > git checkout feature
                > git rebase main
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Creates a **linear history**
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # ⚔️ Key Difference
                > 
                > | Feature | Merge | Rebase |
                > | --- | --- | --- |
                > | History | Preserved (non-linear) | Rewritten (linear) |
                > | Extra commit | ✅ Merge commit | ❌ No extra commit |
                > | Safety | ✅ Safe | ⚠ Can be dangerous |
                > | Readability | ❌ Messy graph | ✅ Clean graph |
            - CHERRY-PICK
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # 🍒 Git Cherry-pick (FULL GUIDE)
                > 
                > ## 🧠 Definition
                > 
                > > **Cherry-pick applies a specific commit from one branch onto another branch.**
                > > 
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick <commit-hash>
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Instead of merging the whole branch, you take **only one commit**
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🎯 When Do You Use It?
                > 
                > Use cherry-pick when you need:
                > 
                > - ✅ A **single fix** from another branch
                > - ✅ A **hotfix in production**
                > - ✅ To avoid merging unwanted changes
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 📊 Example Scenario
                > 
                > ## 🔹 Situation
                > 
                > ```
                > main:     A---B---C
                >                \
                > feature:        D---E
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 You want ONLY commit `E` (not D)
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔹 Command
                > 
                > ```
                > git checkout main
                > git cherry-pick <hash-of-E>
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔹 Result
                > 
                > ```
                > A---B---C---E'   (main)
                >          \
                >           D---E  (feature)
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 `E'` = copied commit (new hash)
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🔥 Real-Life Example (VERY IMPORTANT)
                > 
                > ## 🛠️ Case: Hotfix
                > 
                > - `main` → production
                > - `dev` → ongoing development
                > 
                > 👉 You fix a bug in `dev`, but production is broken
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### ❌ Bad idea:
                > 
                > ```
                > git merge dev
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 brings unfinished features 😱
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### ✅ Correct:
                > 
                > ```
                > git checkout main
                > git cherry-pick <fix-commit>
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Only the fix goes to production
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # ⚙️ Multiple Cherry-pick
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick <commit1> <commit2>
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Apply multiple commits
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## Range cherry-pick
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick A..B
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Applies commits between A and B
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # ⚠️ Conflicts in Cherry-pick
                > 
                > Cherry-pick can cause conflicts (like merge/rebase)
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick <commit>
                > # conflict happens
                > 
                > git add .
                > git cherry-pick--continue
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## Cancel cherry-pick
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick--abort
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # ❗ Important Notes
                > 
                > ## 🔹 1. New Commit Hash
                > 
                > Cherry-picked commit ≠ original commit
                > 
                > 👉 because history is different
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔹 2. Duplicate Changes Risk
                > 
                > If you later merge branches:
                > 
                > - Git may see **duplicate commits**
                > 
                > 👉 can create confusion
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔹 3. Not for Large Features
                > 
                > ❌ Don’t use cherry-pick for:
                > 
                > - full features
                > - big changes
                > 
                > 👉 Use merge/rebase instead
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🧠 Cherry-pick vs Merge
                > 
                > | Feature | Cherry-pick | Merge |
                > | --- | --- | --- |
                > | Scope | Single commit | Whole branch |
                > | History | Copied | Preserved |
                > | Use case | Hotfix | Feature integration |
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 💡 Pro Tips (Interview Level)
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Add commit reference
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick-x <commit>
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Adds:
                > 
                > ```
                > (cherry picked from commit abc123)
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Edit commit while picking
                > 
                > ```
                > git cherry-pick-e <commit>
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Modify message
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🧠 One-Line Interview Answer
                > 
                > > **Cherry-pick allows you to apply a specific commit from one branch onto another without merging the entire branch.**
                > > 
            - RESET vs REVERT
                - RESET TYPES
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ## 3. 🔹 Git Reset Types (VERY IMPORTANT DETAIL)
                    > 
                    > | Type | Effect |
                    > | --- | --- |
                    > | `--soft` | keeps changes staged |
                    > | `--mixed` | keeps changes unstaged |
                    > | `--hard` | deletes everything |
                    > 
                    > 👉 This is a **classic interview trap**
                    > 
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # 🔁 3. Reset vs Revert
                > 
                > ## 🔹 Reset
                > 
                > > **Reset moves the branch pointer to a previous commit** (can delete history).
                > > 
                > 
                > ### 📌 Usage:
                > 
                > ```
                > git reset--hard <commit-hash>
                > ```
                > 
                > ### ⚠️ Important:
                > 
                > - Can remove commits permanently (locally)
                > - Dangerous if already pushed
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔹 Revert
                > 
                > > **Revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit.**
                > > 
                > 
                > ### 📌 Usage:
                > 
                > ```
                > git revert <commit-hash>
                > ```
                > 
                > ### ✅ Safe because:
                > 
                > - Does NOT delete history
                > - Creates a new “undo” commit
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🔥 Key Difference
                > 
                > | Reset | Revert |
                > | --- | --- |
                > | Deletes history | Keeps history |
                > | Changes commit tree | Adds new commit |
                > | Risky | Safe |
            - Stash
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > > **Stash temporarily saves your uncommitted changes** so you can switch branches.
                > > 
                > 
                > ### 📌 Usage:
                > 
                > Save changes:
                > 
                > ```
                > git stash
                > ```
                > 
                > Apply changes back:
                > 
                > ```
                > git stash pop
                > ```
                > 
                > ### ✅ Example:
                > 
                > ```
                > git stash
                > git checkout main
                > git stash pop
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Your work is restored after switching branches
                > 
            - Conflict Resolution
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > > A **conflict** happens when Git cannot automatically merge changes.
                > > 
                > 
                > ### 📌 Example scenario:
                > 
                > - Two branches change the same line in a file
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### 🔥 What Git does:
                > 
                > ```
                > <<<<<<< HEAD
                > your code
                > =======
                > incoming code
                > >>>>>>> branch-name
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### ✅ How to resolve:
                > 
                > 1. Open the file
                > 2. Decide which code to keep (or combine)
                > 3. Remove conflict markers
                > 4. Stage the file:
                > 
                > ```
                > git add <file>
                > ```
                > 
                > 1. Complete merge:
                > 
                > ```
                > git commit
                > ```
                > 
            - GIT internals
                - .GIT/objects
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Everything in Git is stored in the `.git/objects` directory. There are four main types of objects, all identified by a **SHA-1 hash** (a 40-character string).
                    > 
                    > | **Object Type** | **Purpose** | **Content** |
                    > | --- | --- | --- |
                    > | **Blob** | Binary Large Object | Stores the **content** of a file only (no filename). |
                    > | **Tree** | Directory Structure | Acts like a folder. Maps filenames to Blobs or other Trees. |
                    > | **Commit** | Snapshot Metadata | Points to a Root Tree, Parent Commit, Author, and Message. |
                    > | **Tag** | Persistent Mark | A named pointer to a specific commit (e.g., `v1.0`). |
                    > 
                    > > 💡 **Key Concept:** If two files have the exact same content, Git stores only **one blob** and points both filenames to it. This makes Git incredibly space-efficient.
                    > > 
                - **The Three Git States**
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Git moves data between three main areas. Understanding this flow is crucial for mastering internals:
                    > 
                    > 1. **Working Directory:** The actual files you are editing on your disk.
                    > 2. **Staging Area (The Index):** A single binary file at `.git/index` that lists exactly what will go into your next commit.
                    > 3. **Git Directory (Repository):** Where the compressed object database and history live.
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                - **Git References**
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Since remembering hashes like `54e2a7...` is impossible, Git uses "Refs"—simple text files that store a hash.
                    > 
                    > - **Branches:** Found in `.git/refs/heads/`. A branch is just a file containing the hash of the latest commit.
                    > - **HEAD:** A special file (`.git/HEAD`) that tells Git which branch or commit you are currently "standing" on. Usually, it looks like `ref: refs/heads/main`.
                - **Data Compression & Storage**
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > - **Loose Objects:** Initially, every object is stored as a single compressed file.
                    > - **Packfiles:** Periodically (or during a push), Git combines multiple loose objects into a single "Packfile" (`.git/objects/pack/`). It uses **Delta Compression**, storing only the differences between similar versions of a file to save massive amounts of space.
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                - **Plumbing vs. Porcelain**
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > - **Porcelain (User-friendly):** High-level commands like `git add`, `git commit`, and `git pull`.
                    > - **Plumbing (Low-level):** Internal commands used by Git itself, which you can use to inspect the database:
                    >     - `git hash-object`: Computes the SHA-1 for a file.
                    >     - `git cat-file -p <hash>`: Pretty-prints the contents of any Git object.
                    >     - `git ls-files --stage`: Shows exactly what is in the Index.
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
            - LOCAL vs REMOTE REPO
                
                > 
                > 
                > - **Local Repository:** This is the `.git` folder on your actual machine (laptop or PC). It contains your entire history, every branch, and every commit. You have full control here.
                > - **Remote Repository:** This is a version of your project hosted on a server (like **GitHub**, **GitLab**, or a private server). It acts as a central hub where team members share their snapshots.
                > 
                > > **Crucial Difference:** You "commit" to your **Local** repo. You "push" those commits to the **Remote** repo.
                > > 
            - Fetch vs. Pull
                
                > 
                > 
                > - **`git fetch` (The "Safe" Peek):** * It downloads the latest commits and branches from the remote server.
                >     - **It does NOT touch your local work.** It simply updates your local copy of what the remote looks like.
                >     - Use this when you want to see what your teammates have been up to without risking a merge conflict in your current code.
                > - **`git pull` (Fetch + Merge):** * It is a shortcut command. It runs `git fetch` and then immediately runs `git merge` to combine the remote changes into your current local branch.
                >     - **The Risk:** Since it attempts a merge, it can trigger **Merge Conflicts** immediately.
            - PUSH
                
                > 
                > 
                > - **`git push`** is the process of uploading your **Local** commits to the **Remote** repository.
                > - Git will only allow a push if your local branch is up-to-date with the remote. If a teammate has pushed code while you were working, Git will reject your push, forcing you to `pull` (and resolve conflicts) first.
            - Remote-Tracking Branches
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > Remote-tracking branches are "bookmarks" or "read-only" pointers that tell you where a branch was on the remote server the last time you communicated with it.
                > 
                > - They are named using the format `<remote>/<branch>` (e.g., `origin/main` or `origin/feature-login`).
                > - **You cannot move these pointers yourself.** Only Git can move them when you run `fetch`, `pull`, or `push`.
                > - When you run `git status` and see *"Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits,"* Git is comparing your **local `main` pointer** to the **remote-tracking `origin/main` pointer**.
            - HEAD vs Detached HEAD
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > You mentioned HEAD, but not deeply:
                > 
                > - `HEAD` = current commit pointer
                > - Detached HEAD = pointing directly to commit (not branch)
            - Fast-Forward Merge
                - DEFINITION
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ### 📌 Definition
                    > 
                    > A **fast-forward merge** in Git happens when the target branch has **no new commits** since the branch you want to merge was created.
                    > 
                    > 👉 Instead of creating a new merge commit, Git simply **moves the branch pointer forward**.
                    > 
                - USAGE
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ### 🧠 Intuition
                    > 
                    > Think of it like this:
                    > 
                    > > Your branch history is a straight line — no divergence — so Git just “fast-forwards” to the latest commit.
                    > > 
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 📊 Visual Example
                    > 
                    > ### Before Merge
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > main:    A --- B
                    >               \
                    > feature:       C --- D
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Here:
                    > 
                    > - `feature` started from `B`
                    > - `main` did NOT change after `B`
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### After Fast-Forward Merge
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > main:    A --- B --- C --- D
                    > feature:            (same)
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ✅ No merge commit
                    > 
                    > ✅ Clean linear history
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 💻 Sample Commands
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > # Step 1: Switch to main branch
                    > git checkout main
                    > 
                    > # Step 2: Merge feature branch
                    > git merge feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > 👉 Output will look like:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Updating abc123..def456
                    > Fast-forward
                    >  file.js | 2 ++
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ⚠️ When Fast-Forward Happens
                    > 
                    > Fast-forward merge is possible **only if**:
                    > 
                    > ✔ No commits were added to `main` after branching
                    > 
                    > ✔ History is strictly linear
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ❌ When It Does NOT Happen
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > main:    A --- B --- E
                    >               \
                    > feature:       C --- D
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Now `main` has new commit `E` → Git must create a **merge commit** ❌
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🔒 Forcing No Fast-Forward (for clarity in teams)
                    > 
                    > Sometimes teams want to **always keep merge commits**:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > git merge--no-ff feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > 👉 This creates a merge commit even if fast-forward is possible.
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🧠 When to Use Fast-Forward Merge
                    > 
                    > ✔ Small feature branches
                    > 
                    > ✔ You want **clean, linear history**
                    > 
                    > ✔ Solo development or simple workflows
                    > 
                - IMPLEMENTATION
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Alright — let’s make this **practical like a real dev workflow**. I’ll show you how to **simulate both Fast-Forward and 3-Way merge step-by-step** in Git.
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > # ⚡ 1. Fast-Forward Merge — Implementation
                    > 
                    > ### 🧪 Scenario: No divergence (clean history)
                    > 
                    > ### 💻 Commands
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > # Create repo
                    > git init
                    > echo"A" > file.txt
                    > git add .
                    > git commit-m"Initial commit"
                    > 
                    > # Create feature branch
                    > git checkout-b feature
                    > echo"B" >> file.txt
                    > git commit-am"Feature commit 1"
                    > echo"C" >> file.txt
                    > git commit-am"Feature commit 2"
                    > 
                    > # Go back to main (no changes here)
                    > git checkout main
                    > 
                    > # Merge feature → FAST-FORWARD
                    > git merge feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ✅ What Happens
                    > 
                    > - Git sees `main` has **no new commits**
                    > - It just moves pointer forward
                    > 
                    > 👉 Result:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Fast-forward
                    > ```
                    > 
            - 3-way-merge
                - DEFINITION
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ### 📌 Definition
                    > 
                    > ### 3-Way Merge (Git)
                    > 
                    
                    A **3-way merge** in Git happens when two branches have **diverged**, meaning both have new commits after they split.
                    
                - USAGE
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 👉 Git uses **three commits** to perform the merge:
                    > 
                    > 1. **Base (common ancestor)**
                    > 2. **Branch A (e.g., main)**
                    > 3. **Branch B (e.g., feature)**
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🧠 Intuition
                    > 
                    > > Instead of just moving a pointer (like fast-forward), Git compares changes from both branches **relative to a common base**, then combines them.
                    > > 
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 📊 Visual Example
                    > 
                    > ### Before Merge
                    > 
                    > ```
                    >           C --- D   (feature)
                    >          /
                    > A --- B
                    >          \
                    >           E --- F   (main)
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > - `B` = common ancestor
                    > - Both branches added commits → **diverged**
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### After 3-Way Merge
                    > 
                    > ```
                    >           C --- D
                    >          /       \
                    > A --- B           M   (main)
                    >          \       /
                    >           E --- F
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > 👉 `M` = **merge commit** (new commit created by Git)
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 💻 Sample Commands
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > # Step 1: Switch to main
                    > git checkout main
                    > 
                    > # Step 2: Merge feature branch
                    > git merge feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > 👉 Output:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ⚠️ Merge Conflicts (Important)
                    > 
                    > If both branches changed the **same lines**, Git cannot auto-merge:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > <<<<<<<HEAD
                    > console.log("main version");
                    > =======
                    > console.log("feature version");
                    > >>>>>>> feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > 👉 You must manually resolve:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > console.log("final version");
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Then:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > git add .
                    > git commit
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🆚 Fast-Forward vs 3-Way Merge
                    > 
                    > | Feature | Fast-Forward ✅ | 3-Way Merge 🔀 |
                    > | --- | --- | --- |
                    > | New commit created | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
                    > | Branches diverged | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
                    > | History | Linear | Non-linear |
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🧠 When 3-Way Merge Happens
                    > 
                    > ✔ Both branches have commits after split
                    > 
                    > ✔ Parallel development (team work)
                    > 
                    > ✔ Real-world scenarios almost always
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🚀 Pro Insight (Interview Level)
                    > 
                    > - 3-way merge uses **diff algorithm + common ancestor**
                    > - Default strategy in modern Git is **`ort`** (replaced old `recursive`)
                    > - Preserves full history (important for debugging & audit)
                - IMPLEMENTATION
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > # 3-Way Merge — Implementation
                    > 
                    > ### 🧪 Scenario: Branches diverged
                    > 
                    > ### 💻 Commands
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > # Start fresh
                    > git init
                    > echo"A" > file.txt
                    > git add .
                    > git commit-m"Initial commit"
                    > 
                    > # Create feature branch
                    > git checkout-b feature
                    > echo"Feature change" >> file.txt
                    > git commit-am"Feature commit"
                    > 
                    > # Go back to main and make different change
                    > git checkout main
                    > echo"Main change" >> file.txt
                    > git commit-am"Main commit"
                    > 
                    > # Merge feature → 3-WAY MERGE
                    > git merge feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ⚠️ Possible Conflict
                    > 
                    > If both modified same lines, you'll see:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > CONFLICT (content): Merge conflictin file.txt
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 🛠 Resolve Conflict
                    > 
                    > Open file:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > <<<<<<< HEAD
                    > Main change
                    > =======
                    > Feature change
                    > >>>>>>> feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Fix manually:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Main change
                    > Feature change
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Then:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > git add file.txt
                    > git commit-m"Resolved merge conflict"
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### ✅ What Happens
                    > 
                    > - Git uses:
                    >     - base commit
                    >     - main branch
                    >     - feature branch
                    > - Creates a **merge commit**
                    > 
                    > 👉 Result:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Merge made by the'ort' strategy.
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > # 🧠 Key Difference in Commands
                    > 
                    > | Action | Fast-Forward | 3-Way Merge |
                    > | --- | --- | --- |
                    > | `git merge feature` | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
                    > | Extra commits needed? | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
                    > | Conflict possible? | ❌ Rare | ✅ Yes |
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > # 🚀 Pro Tip (Senior Level)
                    > 
                    > You can **control behavior explicitly**:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > # Force fast-forward only (fail if not possible)
                    > git merge--ff-only feature
                    > 
                    > # Force 3-way merge (even if FF possible)
                    > git merge--no-ff feature
                    > ```
                    > 
                
            - AUTOMATIC_MERGE_CONTROL
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # 🧠 Default Behavior (What Git Does)
                > 
                > In Git, when you run:
                > 
                > ```
                > git merge feature
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Git automatically checks the history:
                > 
                > ### ✅ Case 1: No divergence
                > 
                > - Git performs **Fast-Forward merge**
                > 
                > ### 🔀 Case 2: Diverged branches
                > 
                > - Git performs **3-way merge**
                > 
                > So yes — **Git chooses the strategy automatically based on commit graph**.
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🎛️ But You CAN Control It
                > 
                > ### 🔒 Force Fast-Forward ONLY
                > 
                > ```
                > git merge--ff-only feature
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 If FF is not possible → ❌ merge fails
                > 
                > ✔ Useful when you want **strict linear history**
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### 🔀 Force 3-Way Merge (even if FF is possible)
                > 
                > ```
                > git merge--no-ff feature
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 Always creates a **merge commit**
                > 
                > ✔ Useful in teams to:
                > 
                > - preserve feature branch history
                > - make commits easier to track
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ### ⚙️ Set Default Behavior (Config)
                > 
                > You can configure Git globally:
                > 
                > ```
                > # Always create merge commit
                > git config--global merge.fffalse
                > ```
                > 
                > OR
                > 
                > ```
                > # Allow only fast-forward
                > git config--global merge.ff only
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # 🧠 Real-World Insight (Important)
                > 
                > - **Solo / small projects →** Fast-forward is clean ✅
                > - **Teams / production →** often use `-no-ff` 🔀
                > - **Strict workflows →** use `-ff-only` 🔒
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > # ⚡ Final Mental Model
                > 
                > > Git = automatic
                > > 
                > > 
                > > You = control when needed
                > > 
    - DAY-2:WEB_SOCKET,HOSTNAME_vs_DOMAIN_NAME,RELATIONAL DATABASE vs non relational database,N+1 problem,DATABASE MIGRATIONS
        - WEB_SOCKET
            - DEFINITION
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > ## 📌 Definition
                > 
                > A **WebSocket** is a:
                > 
                > > persistent, full-duplex communication channel over a single TCP connection.
                > > 
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🧠 Simple idea
                > 
                > Unlike HTTP:
                > 
                > ```
                > HTTP:
                > client → request → server → response → close
                > ```
                > 
                > WebSocket:
                > 
                > ```
                > client ↔ server (open forever)
                > ```
                > 
                > Both sides can send messages anytime.
                > 
            - WHY EXISTS
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # ⚡ 2. Why WebSocket exists
                > 
                > HTTP is:
                > 
                > - request/response
                > - stateless
                > - expensive for real-time apps
                > 
                > So WebSocket solves:
                > 
                > | Problem | WebSocket solution |
                > | --- | --- |
                > | real-time chat | persistent connection |
                > | live updates | push from server |
                > | low latency | no repeated handshake |
                > | bidirectional | client + server both send |
            - WebSocket lifecycle (VERY IMPORTANT)
                - HTTP UPGRADE (web socket starts as HTTP)
                    - DEFINITION
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > WebSocket starts as HTTP:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > Client → HTTP request
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > Then upgrade:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > Upgrade: websocket
                        > Connection: Upgrade
                        > ```
                        > 
                    - 
                - HANDSHAKE
                    - DEFINITION
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > Server responds:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > 👉 Now HTTP becomes TCP WebSocket tunnel
                        > 
                - Persistent TCP connection
                    - DEFINITION
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > Now:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > TCP socket stays OPEN
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > No more HTTP
                        > 
                    - 
                - Frame-based messaging
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Instead of HTTP requests:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > WebSocket uses FRAMES
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Example:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > [frame 1] "hello"
                    > [frame 2] "update"
                    > ```
                    > 
                - WHERE IS SOCKET IN ARCHITECTURE
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > JavaScript (client/server)
                    > 
                    > ↓
                    > 
                    > WebSocket API
                    > 
                    > ↓
                    > 
                    > Node.js (ws / http upgrade handler)
                    > 
                    > ↓
                    > 
                    > libuv
                    > 
                    > ↓
                    > 
                    > TCP socket
                    > 
                    > ↓
                    > 
                    > OS kernel (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)
                    > 
                - WebSocket inside libuv (IMPORTANT)
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > WebSocket is NOT a special protocol in libuv.
                    > 
                    > It is just:
                    > 
                    > ## 👉 A TCP socket + event callbacks
                    > 
                    > libuv treats it as:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > uv_tcp_t (handle)
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > and:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > uv_poll_t (event watcher)
                    > ```
                    > 
                - How WebSocket works internally
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ## Step-by-step:
                    > 
                    > ### 1. TCP connection created
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > libuv → uv_tcp_init()
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 2. Socket registered with OS
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > epoll / kqueue / IOCP
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > ### 3. Upgrade request arrives
                    > 
                    > HTTP parser detects:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > Upgrade: websocket
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > 
                    
                    ### 4. Handshake accepted
                    
                    Connection stays open:
                    
                    ```
                    socket NOT closed
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 5. Event loop registers socket
                    
                    ```
                    uv__io_poll()
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 6. Data arrives
                    
                    OS triggers:
                    
                    ```
                    "socket readable"
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 7. libuv callback
                    
                    ```
                    data → queue → JS callback
                    ```
                    
                - WebSocket vs HTTP (deep difference)
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > | Feature | HTTP | WebSocket |
                    > | --- | --- | --- |
                    > | connection | short-lived | persistent |
                    > | direction | request/response | full-duplex |
                    > | overhead | high | low |
                    > | transport | TCP | TCP |
                    > | event model | stateless | event-driven |
                - WebSocket event flow (IMPORTANT)
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > OS detects data
                    > ↓
                    > libuv (epoll event)
                    > ↓
                    > socket readable callback
                    > ↓
                    > WebSocket frame parser
                    > ↓
                    > message event emitted
                    > ↓
                    > JS callback executed
                    > 
                - Where event loop fits
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > WebSocket does NOT bypass event loop.
                    > 
                    > It uses:
                    > 
                    > ### libuv poll phase:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > uv__io_poll()
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Then:
                    > 
                    > ### callback scheduling:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > → event loop queue
                    > → JS execution
                    > ```
                    > 
                - Real Node.js example
                    
                    ```jsx
                    import WebSocket from "ws";
                    
                    const wss = new WebSocket.Server({ port: 8080 });
                    
                    wss.on("connection", (socket) => {
                        socket.on("message", (msg) => {
                            console.log("received:", msg.toString());
                            socket.send("hello client");
                        });
                    });
                    Internal execution:
                    TCP socket created (libuv)
                    → epoll watches socket
                    → data arrives
                    → libuv triggers callback
                    → V8 executes "message" handler
                    ```
                    
                - INSIGHT
                    
                    > WebSocket is NOT a new transport layer
                    > 
                    
                    It is:
                    
                    ```
                    HTTP upgrade → TCP socket → event-driven messaging
                    ```
                    
                - WHY WEB SOCKET IS FAST
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Because:
                    > 
                    > - no repeated HTTP handshake
                    > - no headers per request
                    > - persistent TCP connection
                    > - OS-level async notification (epoll)
                - WebSocket internal memory model
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > uv_tcp_t socket
                    > ↓
                    > buffer (incoming data)
                    > ↓
                    > frame parser
                    > ↓
                    > event callbacks
                    > 
                - Scaling WebSocket (REAL SYSTEM PROBLEM)
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > If you have:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > 100,000 connections
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > Then:
                    > 
                    > - 100k sockets in epoll
                    > - 100k file descriptors
                    > - event loop handles readiness only
                    > 
                    > 👉 NOT 100k threads (important)
                    > 
                - BOTTLENECKS
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > WebSocket bottlenecks are NOT CPU
                    > 
                    > They are:
                    > 
                    > - file descriptors limit
                    > - memory per connection
                    > - event loop saturation
                    > - message flood
                - Mental model (senior level)
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Think like this:
                    > 
                    > ```
                    > WebSocket = long-lived TCP pipe
                    > libuv = watches pipe
                    > OS = signals when data arrives
                    > event loop = delivers message to JS
                    > ```
                    > 
                    > ---
                    > 
                    > # 🔥 FINAL SUMMARY
                    > 
                    > > WebSocket is a persistent TCP-based communication channel where libuv uses OS-level event notification (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) to detect socket activity, and the event loop delivers incoming frames to JavaScript callbacks in a fully asynchronous, event-driven model.
                    > > 
                - Q&A
                    - WHAT IF CLIENT IS INACTIVE
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > Good question — this is **exactly where real WebSocket systems start to break in production**, so let’s go deep but clean.
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 💤 1. What does “client is inactive” mean?
                        > 
                        > It can mean different things:
                        > 
                        > ## Case A: Client is idle
                        > 
                        > - App is open
                        > - User not sending/receiving messages
                        > 
                        > ## Case B: Network is dead
                        > 
                        > - Wi-Fi off
                        > - mobile data lost
                        > 
                        > ## Case C: Client is frozen
                        > 
                        > - tab closed
                        > - app crashed
                        > - phone sleeping
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🔁 2. What WebSocket thinks
                        > 
                        > To WebSocket (and TCP):
                        > 
                        > > ❗ “Connection is alive until proven dead”
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > There is **no automatic “inactive detection”**.
                        > 
                        > So if client is silent:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > WebSocket STILL THINKS IT IS CONNECTED
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # ⚙️ 3. What actually happens internally
                        > 
                        > ## If client is idle:
                        > 
                        > - TCP connection stays open
                        > - libuv keeps socket registered in epoll/kqueue
                        > - no events are fired
                        > - memory + file descriptor remain allocated
                        > 
                        > 👉 Nothing happens
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## If client is DEAD (network lost)
                        > 
                        > Now it gets interesting:
                        > 
                        > ### Problem:
                        > 
                        > TCP does NOT immediately know client is gone.
                        > 
                        > So:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > server still believes socket is valid
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > Until one of these happens:
                        > 
                    - HOW TO DETECT  INACTIVE CLIENT
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > ## 🔹 1. TCP Keepalive (OS-level)
                        > 
                        > OS sends tiny probes:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > “Are you alive?”
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > If no response after retries:
                        > 
                        > 👉 connection is dropped
                        > 
                        > ⏱️ This can take minutes to hours (default is slow)
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## 🔹 2. WebSocket Ping/Pong (application-level)
                        > 
                        > This is what real systems use.
                        > 
                        > ### Server sends:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > PING
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ### Client must reply:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > PONG
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > If no response:
                        > 
                        > 👉 server assumes client is dead
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## 🔹 3. Timeout logic (most common)
                        > 
                        > Example:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > if (no messagefor30s → disconnect)
                        > ```
                        > 
                    - What happens in libuv
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > When client is inactive:
                        > 
                        > ### Scenario 1: idle (normal)
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > socket stays in epoll
                        > no callbacks triggered
                        > event loop ignores it
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > 👉 ZERO CPU usage
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ### Scenario 2: dead client
                        > 
                        > Eventually:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > OS detects broken TCP
                        > OR ping timeout fires
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > Then libuv:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > 1. receives socket error event
                        > 2. marks uv_tcp_t as closed
                        > 3. removes from epoll
                        > 4. triggers close callback
                        > ```
                        > 
                    - reconnection signal
                        
                        > 
                        > 
                        > 
                        > # 🔁 1. What “reconnection signal” really means
                        > 
                        > It is NOT:
                        > 
                        > - a WebSocket feature
                        > - a server command
                        > - an OS signal
                        > 
                        > It is:
                        > 
                        > > 🧠 A protocol + client logic that detects disconnect and re-establishes connection
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # ⚙️ 2. When reconnection is triggered
                        > 
                        > Client decides to reconnect when:
                        > 
                        > ## 🔴 1. Connection is closed
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > onclose event fires
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ## 🔴 2. Connection error happens
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > onerror event fires
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ## 🔴 3. Heartbeat fails (PING/PONG timeout)
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > no response from server
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ## 🔴 4. Network changes
                        > 
                        > - Wi-Fi → mobile
                        > - offline → online
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧠 3. Basic reconnection flow
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > WebSocket closes
                        >         ↓
                        > Wait (backoff delay)
                        >         ↓
                        > Create NEW WebSocket
                        >         ↓
                        > Re-authenticate (if needed)
                        >         ↓
                        > Resume session
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧵 4. Simple reconnection implementation (JS)
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > letws;
                        > letretry=0;
                        > 
                        > functionconnect() {
                        > ws=newWebSocket("wss://example.com");
                        > 
                        > ws.onopen= () => {
                        > console.log("connected");
                        > retry=0;
                        >   };
                        > 
                        > ws.onclose= () => {
                        > console.log("disconnected, reconnecting...");
                        > reconnect();
                        >   };
                        > 
                        > ws.onerror= () => {
                        > ws.close();
                        >   };
                        > }
                        > 
                        > functionreconnect() {
                        > retry++;
                        > 
                        > constdelay=Math.min(1000*retry,10000);
                        > 
                        > setTimeout(() => {
                        > connect();
                        >   },delay);
                        > }
                        > 
                        > connect();
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🔥 5. Key idea: exponential backoff
                        > 
                        > Instead of spamming reconnects:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > 1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → 10s cap
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > Why?
                        > 
                        > - avoids server overload
                        > - avoids network flooding
                        > - stabilizes recovery
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # ⚙️ 6. Server-side “reconnection support”
                        > 
                        > Server does NOT send reconnection signal.
                        > 
                        > Instead it helps by:
                        > 
                        > ## ✔ 1. session IDs
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > {
                        >   "type":"auth",
                        >   "sessionId":"abc123"
                        > }
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > So client can resume.
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## ✔ 2. message replay buffer
                        > 
                        > Server may store last messages:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > last 10 messages cached
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > On reconnect:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > client → "resume from last message ID"
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧠 7. Advanced reconnection design (real systems)
                        > 
                        > ## Step 1: detect disconnect
                        > 
                        > - onclose
                        > - ping timeout
                        > - network offline event
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## Step 2: reconnect strategy
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > - exponential backoff
                        > - jitter (random delay)
                        > - max retry limit
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ## Step 3: resubscribe
                        > 
                        > After reconnect:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > rejoin rooms
                        > resubscribe channels
                        > restore state
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧵 8. What happens in libuv during reconnect
                        > 
                        > When reconnect happens:
                        > 
                        > ### OLD connection:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > socket removed from epoll
                        > → uv_close()
                        > → memory freed
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ### NEW connection:
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > new TCP socket created
                        > → registered in epoll
                        > → new uv_tcp_t handle
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > 👉 It is NOT reused — it is a brand new OS socket
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # ⚡ 9. Important truth
                        > 
                        > > WebSocket reconnection is NOT recovery of connection — it is creation of a new connection + state restoration.
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧠 10. Why reconnection is necessary
                        > 
                        > Because WebSocket has:
                        > 
                        > - no guaranteed delivery
                        > - no persistent session
                        > - no automatic recovery
                        > 
                        > So disconnections WILL happen:
                        > 
                        > - Wi-Fi drops
                        > - server restart
                        > - NAT timeout
                        > - mobile switching networks
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🔥 11. Production-grade pattern
                        > 
                        > ```
                        > detect disconnect
                        >     ↓
                        > backoff reconnect
                        >     ↓
                        > re-authenticate
                        >     ↓
                        > restore state
                        >     ↓
                        > resume streaming
                        > ```
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🧠 12. Senior-level insight
                        > 
                        > > WebSocket reliability is not provided by TCP or libuv — it is implemented at the application layer using reconnection + session resumption logic.
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🚨 13. Common mistake
                        > 
                        > ### ❌ Wrong thinking:
                        > 
                        > > “WebSocket will reconnect automatically”
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ### ❌ Wrong thinking:
                        > 
                        > > “server sends reconnect signal”
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > ### ✅ Correct thinking:
                        > 
                        > > client detects failure and re-creates a new socket connection
                        > > 
                        > 
                        > ---
                        > 
                        > # 🔥 FINAL SUMMARY
                        > 
                        > - There is no built-in reconnection signal in WebSocket
                        > - reconnection is handled by the client
                        > - triggers: close, error, heartbeat failure
                        > - implementation uses exponential backoff
                        > - new TCP connection is created each time
                        > - session must be restored manually
        - HOSTNAME_vs_DOMAIN_NAME
            - HOSTNAME_VS_DOMAIN_HOST
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # 🌐 Domain vs Host vs Hostname
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 1. DOMAIN
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Definition
                > 
                > A **domain** is the **human-readable name** used to identify a website on the internet.
                > 
                > 👉 Instead of remembering IP addresses like `142.250.190.78`, we use domains.
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Example
                > 
                > ```
                > google.com
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Key Points
                > 
                > - Managed by DNS (Domain Name System)
                > - Maps to an IP address
                > - Can include subdomains
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 2. HOST
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Definition
                > 
                > A **host** is **any device (server/computer)** connected to a network that can send/receive data.
                > 
                > 👉 It is the **actual machine** behind the domain.
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Example
                > 
                > ```
                > Server with IP: 142.250.190.78
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Key Points
                > 
                > - Physical or virtual machine
                > - Identified by IP address
                > - Runs services (web server, database, etc.)
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 3. HOSTNAME
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Definition
                > 
                > A **hostname** is the **specific name of a host within a domain**.
                > 
                > 👉 It identifies a particular machine or service.
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Example
                > 
                > ```
                > www.google.com
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Breakdown
                > 
                > ```
                > www.google.com
                > │   │      └── Domain (google.com)
                > │   └──────── Subdomain / Hostname
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Key Points
                > 
                > - Part of a full domain name (FQDN)
                > - Points to a specific host
                > - Used in URLs
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 4. FULL COMPARISON
                > 
                > | Term | What it represents | Example |
                > | --- | --- | --- |
                > | Domain | Name of the website | google.com |
                > | Host | Actual machine (server) | 142.250.190.78 |
                > | Hostname | Specific name of a host | www.google.com |
                > 
                > ## 📌 5. HOW THEY CONNECT (VERY IMPORTANT)
                > 
                > ```
                > User types → www.google.com
                >                 ↓
                >          Hostname (www)
                >                 ↓
                >          Domain (google.com)
                >                 ↓
                >          DNS resolves to IP
                >                 ↓
                >          Host (server machine)
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 6. EXTRA (INTERVIEW GOLD 🔥)
                > 
                > - **FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name)**
                >     
                >     ```
                >     www.google.com
                >     ```
                >     
                >     → complete hostname + domain
                >     
                > - **Subdomain = Hostname in many contexts**
                >     
                >     ```
                >     api.google.com
                >     mail.google.com
                >     ```
                >     
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🧠 SIMPLE ANALOGY
                > 
                > Think of it like a house:
                > 
                > - **Domain** → Street name (`google.com`)
                > - **Hostname** → House name (`www`)
                > - **Host** → Actual house (building itself)
            - HOSTNAME_VS_DOMAIN_NAME
                
                > 
                > 
                > 
                > # 🌐 Hostname vs Domain Name
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 DOMAIN NAME
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Definition
                > 
                > A **domain name** is the **main name registered on the internet**.
                > 
                > 👉 It represents your **website identity**.
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Example
                > 
                > ```
                > google.com
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Key Idea
                > 
                > - It is the **base name**
                > - Registered via domain registrars
                > - Used by DNS to map to IP
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 HOSTNAME
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Definition
                > 
                > A **hostname** is the **specific name of a machine or service inside a domain**.
                > 
                > 👉 It identifies **where exactly inside the domain** you want to go.
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Example
                > 
                > ```
                > www.google.com
                > api.google.com
                > mail.google.com
                > ```
                > 
                > ### 🔹 Key Idea
                > 
                > - It is **part of a domain**
                > - Points to a **specific service or server**
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 CORE DIFFERENCE (IMPORTANT)
                > 
                > | Feature | Domain Name | Hostname |
                > | --- | --- | --- |
                > | Meaning | Main website name | Specific machine/service name |
                > | Scope | Broader | More specific |
                > | Example | google.com | www.google.com |
                > | Includes | TLD + name | Subdomain + domain |
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 RELATION (THIS IS THE KEY 🔥)
                > 
                > ```
                > www.google.com
                > │   │      └── Domain (google.com)
                > │   └──────── Hostname (www)
                > ```
                > 
                > 👉 So:
                > 
                > - **Domain = google.com**
                > - **Hostname = www.google.com**
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 📌 SUPER SIMPLE WAY TO THINK
                > 
                > - **Domain name** → “Company name”
                > - **Hostname** → “Department inside company”
                > 
                > Example:
                > 
                > ```
                > google.com       → Company
                > mail.google.com  → Mail department
                > api.google.com   → API department
                > ```
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## ⚠️ COMMON CONFUSION
                > 
                > ✔ Sometimes people say “hostname” when they mean full name
                > 
                > ✔ Technically:
                > 
                > - `google.com` → domain
                > - `www.google.com` → hostname (FQDN)
                > 
                > ---
                > 
                > ## 🧠 INTERVIEW ONE-LINER
                > 
                > 👉 A **domain name** is the base internet name, while a **hostname** is a specific labeled node (machine/service) within that domain.
                >
