                Service Instance 1
                Service Instance 2
                Service Instance 3
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🔁 How it works:
                
                ### Step 1:
                
                User request arrives
                
                ### Step 2:
                
                Load balancer distributes:
                
                ```
                Request → any available service instance
                ```
                
                ### Step 3:
                
                Each service instance:
                
                - processes request
                - queries database
                - returns response
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧠 Key idea:
                
                > Service replicas are “stateless workers”
                > 
                
                They do NOT store permanent data.
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 4. CRITICAL DIFFERENCE (CORE UNDERSTANDING)
                
                | Feature | DB Replication | Service Replication |
                | --- | --- | --- |
                | What is copied | Data | Code |
                | State | Stateful | Stateless (usually) |
                | Sync type | log-based | request-based |
                | Failure recovery | promote replica | restart instance |
                | Scaling goal | data availability | traffic handling |
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 5. VERY IMPORTANT INSIGHT
                
                ## Database replication = “truth replication”
                
                - all replicas must converge to same data
                
                ## Service replication = “capacity replication”
                
                - any instance can serve request
                - no need identical internal state
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 6. CONSISTENCY MODEL DIFFERENCE
                
                ## Database replicas:
                
                Can be:
                
                - strong consistency (rare, expensive)
                - eventual consistency (common in replicas)
                
                👉 data correctness matters
                
                ---
                
                ## Service replicas:
                
                Usually:
                
                ```
                stateless → no consistency problem
                ```
                
                Because state is external (DB, cache)
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 7. FAILURE HANDLING DIFFERENCE
                
                ## Database replication:
                
                If primary dies:
                
                ```
                Replica must be promoted → becomes new leader
                ```
                
                👉 requires consensus (Raft / Paxos in modern systems)
                
                ---
                
                ## Service replication:
                
                If instance dies:
                
                ```
                Load balancer just stops sending traffic
                ```
                
                👉 no recovery needed
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 8. WHY THEY ARE USED TOGETHER
                
                Real systems:
                
                ```
                Service layer (replicated)
                        ↓
                Database layer (replicated)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Example:
                
                - 10 API servers
                - 1 primary DB + 3 replicas
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 9. COMMON CONFUSION (VERY IMPORTANT)
                
                ## ❌ Wrong idea:
                
                > “Service replication protects data”
                > 
                
                No ❌
                
                ---
                
                ## ✔ Correct idea:
                
                - service replication = availability of compute
                - database replication = durability + data availability
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 10. REAL-WORLD PROBLEM EXAMPLE
                
                ## Scenario:
                
                User updates profile:
                
                ### Step 1:
                
                Request hits Service A
                
                ### Step 2:
                
                Service A writes to DB primary
                
                ### Step 3:
                
                Service B reads from DB replica
                
                👉 might see old data
                
                ---
                
                ## This creates:
                
                ```
                READ AFTER WRITE INCONSISTENCY
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 11. ADVANCED INSIGHT (SENIOR LEVEL)
                
                ## System design truth:
                
                > Scaling is split into 2 independent axes:
                > 
                
                ### 1. Compute scaling
                
                - service replication
                
                ### 2. Data scaling
                
                - database replication
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 12. FINAL MENTAL MODEL
                
                ```
                            USERS
                              ↓
                     Load Balancer (routing)
                              ↓
                   ┌──────────────────────┐
                   │ Service Replicas      │  ← stateless compute
                   └──────────────────────┘
                              ↓
                     Database Primary
                              ↓
                   ┌──────────────────────┐
                   │ DB Replicas          │  ← state copies
                   └──────────────────────┘
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 FINAL SUMMARY
                
                ## Database replication =
                
                > “Copying and synchronizing data across machines for durability and availability”
                > 
                
                ## Service replication =
                
                > “Running multiple instances of application logic for handling traffic”
                > 
            - SHARDING
                
                # 🧠 0. CORE IDEA
                
                Sharding =
                
                > **Splitting one large database into multiple smaller databases (shards)**
                > 
                
                Instead of:
                
                ```
                1 huge database
                ```
                
                You do:
                
                ```
                DB → Shard A | Shard B | Shard C
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 1. WHY SHARDING EXISTS
                
                A single database has limits:
                
                - CPU limit
                - RAM limit
                - disk I/O limit
                - connection limit
                
                So when it grows:
                
                ```
                1 billion rows → one machine dies
                ```
                
                Solution:
                
                ```
                split data horizontally → multiple machines
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 2. SHARDING VS REPLICATION (IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE)
                
                | Concept | Meaning |
                | --- | --- |
                | Replication | same data copied |
                | Sharding | data split |
                
                ---
                
                ## Example:
                
                ### Replication:
                
                ```
                Shard A = full copy
                Shard B = full copy
                Shard C = full copy
                ```
                
                ### Sharding:
                
                ```
                Shard A → users 1–1M
                Shard B → users 1M–2M
                Shard C → users 2M–3M
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 3. SHARDING ARCHITECTURE
                
                ```
                             CLIENT
                                ↓
                        SHARD ROUTER (CRITICAL)
                         ↓      ↓      ↓
                      Shard1  Shard2  Shard3
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 4. SHARD ROUTER (THE BRAIN)
                
                This is the most important component.
                
                It decides:
                
                > “Which shard holds this data?”
                > 
                
                ---
                
                ## Simple implementation:
                
                ```
                defget_shard(user_id):
                returnuser_id%3
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Example:
                
                ```
                user_id = 7 → shard 1
                user_id = 8 → shard 2
                user_id = 9 → shard 0
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 5. SHARDING STRATEGIES
                
                ---
                
                # 🟢 5.1 HORIZONTAL SHARDING (MOST COMMON)
                
                Split rows:
                
                ```
                Users table:
                → shard by user_id
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                Shard 1 → users 1–100k
                Shard 2 → users 100k–200k
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔵 5.2 VERTICAL SHARDING
                
                Split columns:
                
                ```
                User DB:
                - shard 1 → user info (name, email)
                - shard 2 → user analytics (logs, stats)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🟡 5.3 HASH-BASED SHARDING
                
                ```
                shard = hash(user_id) % N
                ```
                
                ✔ even distribution
                
                ❌ hard to reshard later
                
                ---
                
                # 🟣 5.4 RANGE-BASED SHARDING
                
                ```
                1–100k → shard 1
                100k–200k → shard 2
                ```
                
                ✔ easy to understand
                
                ❌ hotspot risk
                
                ---
                
                # 🟠 5.5 CONSISTENT HASHING (ADVANCED)
                
                Used in:
                
                - Redis clusters
                - DynamoDB
                - Cassandra
                
                ---
                
                ## Idea:
                
                Instead of % N:
                
                ```
                hash ring → nodes placed on circle
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ### Flow:
                
                ```
                data → hash → position on ring → nearest node clockwise
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Why this matters:
                
                When adding a shard:
                
                ```
                only small portion of data moves
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 6. SHARDING PROBLEMS (REAL WORLD PAIN)
                
                ---
                
                # 💥 6.1 CROSS-SHARD QUERIES
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                SELECT*FROM usersJOIN orders
                ```
                
                Problem:
                
                ```
                users in shard 1
                orders in shard 3
                ```
                
                👉 JOIN becomes distributed network operation ❌ slow
                
                ---
                
                # 💥 6.2 SHARD HOTSPOTS
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                user_id % 3
                ```
                
                But:
                
                - some users generate 90% traffic
                
                👉 shard overload
                
                ---
                
                # 💥 6.3 RESHARDING (HARD PROBLEM)
                
                When you add a new shard:
                
                ```
                old distribution breaks
                ```
                
                Now you must:
                
                ```
                move huge amount of data
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 💥 6.4 GLOBAL TRANSACTIONS
                
                Problem:
                
                ```
                update shard A + shard B together
                ```
                
                👉 ACID across shards is hard
                
                Solutions:
                
                - 2PC (Two-phase commit)
                - Saga pattern
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 7. REAL SYSTEM DESIGN FLOW
                
                ## WRITE FLOW:
                
                ```
                Client
                  ↓
                Shard Router
                  ↓
                Correct Shard DB
                  ↓
                Write + WAL + Storage
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## READ FLOW:
                
                ```
                Client
                  ↓
                Shard Router
                  ↓
                Find correct shard
                  ↓
                Fetch data
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 8. SHARDING + REPLICATION TOGETHER
                
                Real systems combine both:
                
                ```
                Shard 1 → Replica A, B
                Shard 2 → Replica C, D
                Shard 3 → Replica E, F
                ```
                
                So:
                
                - sharding = split data
                - replication = copy each shard
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 9. REAL WORLD EXAMPLES
                
                | System | Sharding strategy |
                | --- | --- |
                | MongoDB | range + hash |
                | Cassandra | consistent hashing |
                | MySQL clusters | application-level sharding |
                | DynamoDB | managed hashing |
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 10. SIMPLE MENTAL MODEL
                
                ## Without sharding:
                
                ```
                1 DB = 100% load
                ```
                
                ## With sharding:
                
                ```
                3 DBs = 33% load each
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 11. FINAL ENGINEERING INSIGHT
                
                Sharding is NOT:
                
                ```
                “splitting database” ❌
                ```
                
                It is:
                
                ```
                “routing system + distributed data ownership model” ✔
                ```
                
            - 🧱 NoSQL Scaling (Deep Dive)
                
                NoSQL databases (like MongoDB, Cassandra, Dynamo-style systems) are built with one main idea:
                
                > 👉 **Scale horizontally first, consistency later (or optionally)**
                > 
                
                ---
                
                # ⚙️ 1. WHY NoSQL SCALING EXISTS
                
                Traditional SQL databases:
                
                ```
                Scale = stronger CPU + more RAM (vertical scaling)
                ```
                
                Problem:
                
                - one machine limit
                - expensive
                - single bottleneck
                
                NoSQL idea:
                
                ```
                Scale = add more machines (horizontal scaling)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 2. CORE SCALING STRATEGIES
                
                NoSQL scales using 3 main mechanisms:
                
                ```
                1. Replication
                2. Sharding
                3. Partitioning strategy
                ```
                
                We go step-by-step.
                
                ---
                
                # 🪞 3. REPLICATION (DATA COPIES)
                
                ## 📌 Idea:
                
                Same data exists on multiple machines:
                
                ```
                Node A (Primary)
                Node B (Replica)
                Node C (Replica)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🔁 Write flow:
                
                ```
                Client → Primary node
                        ↓
                   replicate changes
                        ↓
                Replica nodes updated
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 📖 Read flow:
                
                Depends on config:
                
                ### Option 1: Strong consistency
                
                ```
                Read only from Primary
                ```
                
                ### Option 2: Eventual consistency
                
                ```
                Read from any replica
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 💥 Why replication exists:
                
                - fault tolerance
                - high availability
                - read scaling
                
                ---
                
                ## ⚠️ Problem:
                
                Replication lag:
                
                ```
                Primary updated → replica still old for milliseconds/seconds
                ```
                
                👉 leads to stale reads
                
                ---
                
                # 🍰 4. SHARDING (HORIZONTAL PARTITIONING)
                
                This is the MOST important scaling concept.
                
                ---
                
                ## 📌 Idea:
                
                Split data across multiple machines:
                
                ```
                Users 1–1M → Node A
                Users 1M–2M → Node B
                Users 2M–3M → Node C
                ```
                
                Each node = shard
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧠 How routing works:
                
                There is usually a **shard key**
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                user_id
                ```
                
                Then:
                
                ```
                hash(user_id) → decides shard
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## ⚙️ Sharding flow:
                
                ```
                Client
                  ↓
                Router / Coordinator
                  ↓
                Correct shard selected
                  ↓
                Data returned
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 💥 Why sharding exists:
                
                - removes single-node limit
                - distributes load
                - increases storage capacity
                
                ---
                
                # 🧨 5. SHARDING STRATEGIES
                
                ## 1. Range-based sharding
                
                ```
                A–F → Node 1
                G–M → Node 2
                N–Z → Node 3
                ```
                
                ✔ easy
                
                ❌ hot partitions
                
                ---
                
                ## 2. Hash-based sharding (most common)
                
                ```
                hash(user_id) % N
                ```
                
                ✔ balanced
                
                ✔ scalable
                
                ❌ hard resharding
                
                ---
                
                ## 3. Geo / location-based
                
                ```
                EU users → EU shard
                US users → US shard
                ```
                
                ✔ low latency
                
                ❌ uneven load
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 6. REPLICATION + SHARDING TOGETHER
                
                Real systems combine both:
                
                ```
                Shard 1 → replicated (A1, A2, A3)
                Shard 2 → replicated (B1, B2, B3)
                Shard 3 → replicated (C1, C2, C3)
                ```
                
                So:
                
                - sharding = split data
                - replication = copy each split
                
                ---
                
                # ⚡ 7. CONSISTENCY MODELS
                
                NoSQL scaling forces trade-offs:
                
                ## 🧠 CAP theorem:
                
                You can only fully guarantee 2:
                
                ```
                C = Consistency
                A = Availability
                P = Partition tolerance
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## In practice:
                
                ### MongoDB-style:
                
                - strong consistency possible
                - replication-based
                
                ### Cassandra-style:
                
                - high availability
                - eventual consistency
                
                ---
                
                # 🔁 8. EVENTUAL CONSISTENCY (IMPORTANT)
                
                Meaning:
                
                ```
                System becomes consistent over time
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                Write → node A
                      → node B updates after 200ms
                      → node C updates after 500ms
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 9. FAILURE HANDLING
                
                ## If a node dies:
                
                ### Replication system:
                
                ```
                Replica promoted → becomes primary
                ```
                
                ### Sharding system:
                
                ```
                Shard recreated from replica
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚙️ 10. DATA RESHARDING (HARD PART)
                
                When cluster grows:
                
                ```
                Need to redistribute data
                ```
                
                Problem:
                
                ```
                moving TBs of data without downtime
                ```
                
                Solutions:
                
                - consistent hashing
                - virtual nodes (vNodes)
                - background migration
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 11. CONSISTENT HASHING (KEY IDEA)
                
                Instead of:
                
                ```
                hash % N
                ```
                
                Use:
                
                ```
                ring-based mapping
                ```
                
                So when node is added:
                
                - only small portion of data moves
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 12. REAL SYSTEM FLOW (FULL VIEW)
                
                ```
                Client Request
                   ↓
                Load Balancer / Router
                   ↓
                Shard selection (hash / range)
                   ↓
                Primary node
                   ↓
                Replication to replicas
                   ↓
                Write acknowledged
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🚀 FINAL MENTAL MODEL
                
                NoSQL scaling = 3 layers:
                
                ```
                1. Sharding → split data horizontally
                2. Replication → copy data for safety
                3. Routing → decide where request goes
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 SENIOR INSIGHT
                
                Why NoSQL scales better:
                
                - avoids single writer bottleneck
                - distributes disk + CPU
                - relaxes consistency rules
                
                Why SQL is harder to scale:
                
                - joins across shards are expensive
                - strict ACID constraints
                - global consistency required
            - AWS auto scaling
                
                Auto Scaling in AWS is not “one feature” — it’s a **system of multiple mechanisms working together** to keep your application stable under changing load.
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 1. WHAT AUTO SCALING REALLY MEANS
                
                > 👉 Automatically adjust compute capacity based on demand
                > 
                
                In AWS, it usually means:
                
                ```
                More traffic → add servers
                Less traffic → remove servers
                ```
                
                This mainly applies to:
                
                - EC2 instances
                - containers (ECS/EKS)
                - sometimes Lambda (built-in scaling)
                
                Core service:
                
                - Amazon Web Services Auto Scaling Group (ASG)
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 2. CORE COMPONENTS
                
                AWS Auto Scaling is built from 3 main parts:
                
                ```
                1. Launch Template / Configuration
                2. Auto Scaling Group (ASG)
                3. Scaling Policies
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧱 (1) Launch Template
                
                Defines:
                
                - AMI (OS image)
                - instance type (t2.micro, etc.)
                - security groups
                - startup script (user data)
                
                👉 Think:
                
                ```
                Blueprint of a server
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧱 (2) Auto Scaling Group (ASG)
                
                This is the **brain controller**
                
                It defines:
                
                ```
                - minimum instances
                - desired instances
                - maximum instances
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                Min = 2
                Desired = 4
                Max = 10
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧱 (3) Scaling Policies
                
                Rules that decide WHEN to scale.
                
                ---
                
                # ⚙️ 3. TYPES OF AUTO SCALING
                
                ## 📈 1. Dynamic Scaling (most important)
                
                Scale based on metrics.
                
                ### Common metrics:
                
                - CPU utilization
                - memory usage
                - request count
                - latency
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                IF CPU > 70% → add 1 instance
                IF CPU < 30% → remove 1 instance
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## ⏰ 2. Scheduled Scaling
                
                Scale at fixed times:
                
                ```
                8 AM → increase capacity
                10 PM → reduce capacity
                ```
                
                Used for predictable traffic (schools, business apps)
                
                ---
                
                ## 🤖 3. Predictive Scaling
                
                AWS uses ML:
                
                ```
                Analyzes past traffic → predicts future load
                ```
                
                So it scales BEFORE traffic hits.
                
                ---
                
                # 🔁 4. HOW AUTO SCALING WORKS INTERNALLY
                
                Let’s go step-by-step:
                
                ```
                1. CloudWatch collects metrics
                2. Metric crosses threshold
                3. Scaling policy triggers
                4. ASG decides add/remove instances
                5. EC2 instances launched or terminated
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🧠 FULL FLOW:
                
                ```
                User Traffic
                   ↓
                Load Balancer (ELB)
                   ↓
                EC2 Instances (ASG)
                   ↓
                CloudWatch monitors metrics
                   ↓
                Scaling decision
                   ↓
                Launch / Terminate EC2
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚖️ 5. LOAD BALANCER ROLE (CRITICAL)
                
                Usually:
                
                - Application Load Balancer (ALB)
                
                It:
                
                ```
                Distributes traffic evenly across instances
                ```
                
                When new instance joins:
                
                ```
                ALB automatically includes it
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧨 6. SCALE OUT vs SCALE IN
                
                ## 📈 Scale OUT
                
                ```
                Add more instances
                ```
                
                Triggered when:
                
                - high CPU
                - high latency
                - traffic spike
                
                ---
                
                ## 📉 Scale IN
                
                ```
                Remove instances
                ```
                
                Triggered when:
                
                - low CPU
                - low traffic
                
                ---
                
                # ⚠️ 7. COOL DOWN PERIOD (VERY IMPORTANT)
                
                After scaling:
                
                ```
                Wait X minutes before next scaling action
                ```
                
                Why?
                
                👉 Prevents:
                
                - rapid scaling loops
                - instability
                - cost spikes
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 8. HEALTH CHECKS
                
                ASG constantly checks instances:
                
                ### If instance fails:
                
                ```
                Terminate instance
                Launch new one automatically
                ```
                
                Types:
                
                - EC2 health check
                - ELB health check (better)
                
                ---
                
                # 🧱 9. DESIRED STATE MODEL
                
                ASG works like this:
                
                ```
                You define desired capacity
                AWS maintains it automatically
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                Desired = 4
                ```
                
                If one dies:
                
                ```
                AWS launches new one → restores 4
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 10. REAL WORLD ARCHITECTURE
                
                ```
                        Internet
                           ↓
                    Load Balancer (ALB)
                           ↓
                   Auto Scaling Group
                     ↓      ↓      ↓
                   EC2    EC2    EC2
                     ↓      ↓      ↓
                   App running horizontally
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚡ 11. WHY AUTO SCALING IS POWERFUL
                
                It gives:
                
                ### 1. High availability
                
                - system survives instance failure
                
                ### 2. Elasticity
                
                - handles traffic spikes
                
                ### 3. Cost optimization
                
                - no over-provisioning
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 12. COMMON SCALING STRATEGIES
                
                ## 🔥 Target Tracking (BEST)
                
                ```
                Keep CPU at 50%
                ```
                
                AWS automatically adjusts instances.
                
                ---
                
                ## 📊 Step Scaling
                
                ```
                CPU > 70% → +1 instance
                CPU > 90% → +3 instances
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 🎯 Simple Scaling
                
                Old method (less used)
                
                ---
                
                # 🧨 13. COMMON PROBLEMS
                
                ## 1. Cold start delay
                
                ```
                New instance takes time to boot
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 2. Over-scaling
                
                Too many instances = wasted cost
                
                ---
                
                ## 3. Under-scaling
                
                Slow system under sudden load
                
                ---
                
                ## 4. State issues
                
                Instances are stateless in ideal design
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 14. IMPORTANT DESIGN RULE
                
                Auto Scaling ONLY works well if:
                
                ```
                Application is stateless
                ```
                
                Meaning:
                
                - no session stored in memory
                - no local dependency
                
                Sessions should go to:
                
                - Redis
                - DB
                - external store
                
                ---
                
                # 🚀 FINAL MENTAL MODEL
                
                ```
                Traffic ↑
                   ↓
                Load Balancer
                   ↓
                Auto Scaling Group
                   ↓
                EC2 instances dynamically adjust
                   ↓
                CloudWatch monitors everything
                   ↓
                Scaling policies react automatically
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 SENIOR INSIGHT
                
                Auto Scaling is NOT about “adding servers”
                
                It is about:
                
                ```
                Keeping latency stable under unpredictable load
                while minimizing cost
                ```
                
            - SCALING HORIZONAL VS VERTICAL
                - DEFINIITON
                    
                    > This is where the architectural philosophies truly diverge. Relational databases traditionally scale *vertically* (bigger machine); NoSQL was designed to scale *horizontally* (more machines).
                    > 
                - VISUALIZATION
                    
                    > 
                    > 
                    > 
                    > ![image.png](DOCUMENTATIONS/image%2023.png)
                    > 
                - IMPLEMENTATION
                    - VERTICAL
                        - PROS_vs_CONS
                            
                            > 
                            > 
                            > 
                            > # Vertical Scaling (Scale UP)
                            > 
                            > ## 💡 Core Idea
                            > 
                            > You **increase resources of ONE machine**:
                            > 
                            > - More CPU cores
                            > - More RAM
                            > - Faster disk (SSD → NVMe)
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ## 🔧 How It’s Actually Implemented
                            > 
                            > ### 1. Infrastructure Layer
                            > 
                            > You literally resize the machine:
                            > 
                            > - On cloud (e.g. Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform):
                            >     - Stop instance
                            >     - Change instance type
                            >     - Restart
                            > 
                            > Example:
                            > 
                            > ```
                            > t2.medium → t2.2xlarge
                            > ```
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ### 2. OS + Kernel Behavior
                            > 
                            > The OS automatically:
                            > 
                            > - Detects new CPU cores
                            > - Expands memory usage
                            > 
                            > But here’s the catch:
                            > 
                            > 👉 Your app **must support multi-threading**
                            > 
                            > Otherwise:
                            > 
                            > - 1 core used
                            > - Other cores idle ❌
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ### 3. Application-Level Constraints
                            > 
                            > Vertical scaling works well only if:
                            > 
                            > - Your app is:
                            >     - multi-threaded
                            >     - or async (like Node.js)
                            > 
                            > Example:
                            > 
                            > - Node.js uses:
                            >     - **event loop + libuv thread pool**
                            >     - Not full CPU scaling → limited benefit from more cores
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ### 4. Database Vertical Scaling
                            > 
                            > For DBs (like PostgreSQL):
                            > 
                            > - Increase:
                            >     - shared_buffers
                            >     - work_mem
                            >     - CPU parallel workers
                            > 
                            > But still:
                            > 
                            > - Single machine bottleneck remains
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ## 🚨 Real Problems (VERY IMPORTANT)
                            > 
                            > ### ❌ 1. Hardware Limits
                            > 
                            > You can’t go beyond:
                            > 
                            > - Max RAM
                            > - Max CPU supported
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ### ❌ 2. Downtime Required
                            > 
                            > Most upgrades:
                            > 
                            > - Require restart
                            > - → service interruption
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ### ❌ 3. Single Point of Failure
                            > 
                            > If the machine dies:
                            > 
                            > ```
                            > SYSTEM DOWN ❌
                            > ```
                            > 
                            > ---
                            > 
                            > ## 📊 When Vertical Scaling is Used
                            > 
                            > - Early-stage startups
                            > - Simple monolith apps
                            > - Databases (initial phase)
                        - Q&A
                            - WHAT IS SHARED BUFFER IN POSTGRES
                                
                                > 
                                > 
                                > 
                                > `shared_buffers` is:
                                > 
                                > > **A chunk of RAM that PostgreSQL allocates to cache data pages (table + index data) for faster access.**
                                > > 
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 🔍 Think of it like this
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Disk (slow)  →  shared_buffers (fast RAM)  →  Query execution
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 Instead of reading from disk every time, PostgreSQL:
                                > 
                                > - Loads data into `shared_buffers`
                                > - Reuses it for future queries
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ What exactly is stored inside?
                                > 
                                > Postgres works with **pages** (not rows directly)
                                > 
                                > - Page size = **8 KB**
                                > - Everything is split into pages:
                                >     - Table data
                                >     - Index data
                                > 
                                > Inside `shared_buffers`:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > [ Page 1 ][ Page 2 ][ Page 3 ] ...
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔁 How it works (REAL FLOW)
                                > 
                                > ### 1. Query comes in
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SELECT*FROM usersWHERE id=10;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 2. PostgreSQL checks `shared_buffers`
                                > 
                                > - If page is there → ✅ **CACHE HIT**
                                > - If not → ❌ **CACHE MISS**
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 3. If CACHE MISS
                                > 
                                > - Read page from disk
                                > - Load into `shared_buffers`
                                > - Then process query
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 4. If CACHE HIT
                                > 
                                > - Directly read from memory (MUCH faster)
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🚀 Why it’s IMPORTANT
                                > 
                                > ### ⚡ Performance boost
                                > 
                                > RAM is:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > ~100x faster than disk
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > So:
                                > 
                                > - More `shared_buffers` → fewer disk reads → faster queries
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 🧠 Reduces I/O bottleneck
                                > 
                                > Disk I/O is the **slowest part** of DB systems
                                > 
                                > This cache minimizes that
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚖️ How PostgreSQL manages it internally
                                > 
                                > Postgres uses a **buffer manager**
                                > 
                                > ### Replacement strategy:
                                > 
                                > - Approximation of **LRU (Least Recently Used)**
                                > 
                                > Meaning:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Recently used → stays
                                > Old unused → evicted
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧩 Important detail (VERY IMPORTANT)
                                > 
                                > 👉 `shared_buffers` is **NOT the only cache**
                                > 
                                > There are 2 layers:
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 1. PostgreSQL cache
                                > 
                                > - `shared_buffers`
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 2. OS page cache (Linux kernel)
                                > 
                                > Even if Postgres misses:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers → miss
                                > OS cache → hit (still fast)
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧨 Common misunderstanding
                                > 
                                > ❌ “Just increase shared_buffers as much as possible”
                                > 
                                > 👉 WRONG
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## Why?
                                > 
                                > Because:
                                > 
                                > - OS also needs RAM for caching
                                > - Too large `shared_buffers`:
                                >     - Starves OS cache
                                >     - Can reduce performance
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 📊 Recommended size
                                > 
                                > General rule:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers = 25% of total RAM
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Example:
                                > 
                                > - 16 GB RAM → 4 GB shared_buffers
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ Example config
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers = 4GB
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Advanced Insight (Senior Level)
                                > 
                                > ### Dirty Pages
                                > 
                                > When data changes:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers (modified) ≠ disk
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > These are called:
                                > 
                                > 👉 **dirty buffers**
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### Background writer + Checkpointer
                                > 
                                > Postgres writes them to disk using:
                                > 
                                > - Background writer
                                > - Checkpointer
                                > 
                                > → avoids blocking queries
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚔️ Real-world behavior
                                > 
                                > ### Scenario 1: Small `shared_buffers`
                                > 
                                > - Many disk reads ❌
                                > - Slow queries
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### Scenario 2: Optimal size
                                > 
                                > - High cache hit ratio ✅
                                > - Fast system
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### Scenario 3: Too large
                                > 
                                > - OS cache reduced ❌
                                > - Memory pressure
                                > - Performance drops
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Final Mental Model
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers = PostgreSQL’s private RAM cache
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > - Stores **pages**
                                > - Avoids disk access
                                > - Managed by Postgres itself
                                > - Works together with OS cache
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔥 Interview-level answer
                                > 
                                > If someone asks:
                                > 
                                > > “What is shared_buffers?”
                                > > 
                                > 
                                > You say:
                                > 
                                > > It’s PostgreSQL’s internal memory cache that stores frequently accessed data pages to reduce disk I/O and improve query performance, managed by its buffer manager using an LRU-like strategy.
                                > > 
                            - WHAT IS work_mem
                                
                                > 
                                > 
                                > 
                                > > `work_mem` is the amount of memory **allocated per operation (not per query)** for **sorting, hashing, and intermediate query processing**.
                                > > 
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔍 Key idea (THIS CHANGES EVERYTHING)
                                > 
                                > 👉 It is **NOT global memory**
                                > 
                                > 👉 It is **NOT per query**
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > It is per operation, per query, per connection
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ Where `work_mem` is used
                                > 
                                > Whenever PostgreSQL needs to:
                                > 
                                > ### 1. Sorting
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > ORDERBY
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 2. Hashing
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > HASHJOIN
                                > GROUPBY
                                > DISTINCT
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 3. Aggregations
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > COUNT(), SUM(), AVG()
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔁 Real execution example
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SELECT*
                                > FROM orders
                                > ORDERBY created_at;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 PostgreSQL:
                                > 
                                > - Allocates `work_mem`
                                > - Performs sort in memory (if enough space)
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🚨 What if `work_mem` is NOT enough?
                                > 
                                > Then:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > RAM → FULL ❌
                                > ↓
                                > Disk spill (temporary files) 💀
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Postgres writes to disk:
                                > 
                                > - MUCH slower
                                > - Huge performance drop
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 💣 WHY this is dangerous
                                > 
                                > Let’s say:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > work_mem = 64MB
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Looks safe, right?
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## ❗ Now imagine:
                                > 
                                > - 100 users connected
                                > - Each query uses:
                                >     - 2 sorts
                                >     - 1 hash join
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > 100 × 3 × 64MB = 19.2 GB RAM 😳
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 You just crashed your server.
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Compare with `shared_buffers`
                                > 
                                > | Feature | shared_buffers | work_mem |
                                > | --- | --- | --- |
                                > | Scope | Global | Per operation |
                                > | Purpose | Cache data pages | Query processing |
                                > | Risk | Low | VERY HIGH |
                                > | Managed by | Postgres buffer manager | Query executor |
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ Internal behavior
                                > 
                                > ## Case 1: Enough memory
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Sort in RAM ✅
                                > Fast
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## Case 2: Not enough
                                > 
                                > Postgres uses:
                                > 
                                > 👉 **External merge sort**
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Split → Write to disk → Merge
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Very slow.
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔬 Hash operations
                                > 
                                > For queries like:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SELECT*
                                > FROM users u
                                > JOIN orders oON u.id= o.user_id;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 PostgreSQL may use:
                                > 
                                > - **Hash Join**
                                > 
                                > It builds a hash table in memory using `work_mem`.
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🚨 If memory is exceeded
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Hash table → spilled to disk ❌
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > → destroys performance
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 📊 Recommended values
                                > 
                                > There is NO universal value, but:
                                > 
                                > ### Safe starting point:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > work_mem = 4MB – 16MB
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### High-performance systems:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > work_mem = 32MB – 128MB (carefully!)
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Advanced tuning strategy
                                > 
                                > Instead of global increase:
                                > 
                                > 👉 Set per query:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SET work_mem='128MB';
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 🔥 Example (smart usage)
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SET work_mem='256MB';
                                > 
                                > SELECT*
                                > FROM huge_table
                                > ORDERBY big_column;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 Only this query gets high memory
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧩 Real-world insight
                                > 
                                > ### OLTP systems (many small queries)
                                > 
                                > - Keep `work_mem` LOW
                                > - Avoid memory explosion
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### OLAP systems (analytics)
                                > 
                                > - Increase `work_mem`
                                > - Heavy queries benefit
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧨 Hidden multiplier (IMPORTANT)
                                > 
                                > Each of these uses its own `work_mem`:
                                > 
                                > - Sort
                                > - Hash Join
                                > - Aggregate
                                > - Subquery
                                > 
                                > 👉 One query can use:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > work_mem × multiple times
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Final mental model
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > shared_buffers → caching data
                                > work_mem → processing data
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔥 Interview-level answer
                                > 
                                > > `work_mem` is a per-operation memory setting in PostgreSQL used for sorting, hashing, and aggregations. If exceeded, PostgreSQL spills to disk, significantly slowing down queries. Misconfiguration can lead to memory exhaustion because it is allocated per operation per connection.
                                > > 
                            - CPU parallel workers
                                
                                > 
                                > 
                                > 
                                > > **Parallel workers** are background processes that PostgreSQL spawns to execute parts of a query **simultaneously across multiple CPU cores**.
                                > > 
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔍 Core idea
                                > 
                                > Instead of:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > 1 query → 1 CPU core ❌
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Postgres can do:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > 1 query → multiple CPU cores ✅
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ How it actually works (REAL FLOW)
                                > 
                                > ### Example query:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SELECT*FROM orders;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## Without parallelism
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Main process → scans entire table alone
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## With parallel workers
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Main process (leader)
                                >    ↓
                                > Splits work
                                >    ↓
                                > Worker 1 → scan part 1
                                > Worker 2 → scan part 2
                                > Worker 3 → scan part 3
                                >    ↓
                                > Merge results
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧩 Types of Parallel Operations
                                > 
                                > PostgreSQL can parallelize:
                                > 
                                > ### 1. Parallel Sequential Scan
                                > 
                                > - Large table split into chunks
                                > - Each worker scans a portion
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 2. Parallel Join
                                > 
                                > - Workers process join in parallel
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 3. Parallel Aggregation
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > SELECTCOUNT(*)FROM big_table;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > - Each worker counts subset
                                > - Final result merged
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### 4. Parallel Index Scan (limited cases)
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚙️ Key Configuration Parameters
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 1. `max_worker_processes`
                                > 
                                > 👉 Total background workers allowed
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > max_worker_processes = 8
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 2. `max_parallel_workers`
                                > 
                                > 👉 Total workers for parallel queries
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > max_parallel_workers = 8
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 3. `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`
                                > 
                                > 👉 Workers per single query
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## 4. `parallel_setup_cost` & `parallel_tuple_cost`
                                > 
                                > 👉 Control when parallelism is used
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🔁 Execution Node: “Gather”
                                > 
                                > In execution plan you’ll see:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Gather
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 This is where:
                                > 
                                > - Results from workers are collected
                                > - Combined into final output
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧠 Leader + Workers Model
                                > 
                                > - **Leader process**:
                                >     - Coordinates
                                >     - May also do work
                                > - **Workers**:
                                >     - Execute parts of query
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🚀 When Parallelism is Triggered
                                > 
                                > Postgres decides automatically based on:
                                > 
                                > - Table size (large tables only)
                                > - Query cost
                                > - Available CPUs
                                > - Configuration
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ❌ When it DOES NOT work
                                > 
                                > Parallelism is disabled if:
                                > 
                                > - Small tables
                                > - Queries are too simple
                                > - Functions are not parallel-safe
                                > - Transactions restrict it
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 🧨 Real limitations (IMPORTANT)
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## ❌ 1. Overhead cost
                                > 
                                > Creating workers is expensive:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Spawn process → setup → coordinate
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > 👉 For small queries → slower ❌
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## ❌ 2. Not all queries benefit
                                > 
                                > - Index lookups → usually single-threaded
                                > - OLTP queries → little benefit
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## ❌ 3. Contention
                                > 
                                > Too many workers:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > CPU contention → slowdown
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ## ❌ 4. Memory multiplication
                                > 
                                > Each worker may use:
                                > 
                                > - its own `work_mem`
                                > 
                                > 👉 Memory usage explodes 💀
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # 📊 Real Example
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > EXPLAIN ANALYZE
                                > SELECTCOUNT(*)FROM orders;
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > Output:
                                > 
                                > ```
                                > Gather
                                >   Workers Planned: 4
                                >   Workers Launched: 4
                                > ```
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > # ⚖️ When to use it
                                > 
                                > ### ✅ Good for:
                                > 
                                > - Large table scans
                                > - Analytics (OLAP)
                                > - Aggregations
                                > 
                                > ---
                                > 
                                > ### ❌ Bad for:
                                > 
                                > - Small queries
                                > - High-concurrency systems (OLTP)
                                > 
                                > ---
                                >
