        - argon2
            - What is this
                
                # 🧠 What is Argon2?
                
                👉 Argon2 is the **modern password hashing algorithm**
                
                👉 Winner of the **Password Hashing Competition (PHC)**
                
                ```
                password → Argon2 → secure hash
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 Why Argon2 exists
                
                Problems with older ones:
                
                ```
                bcrypt → only CPU-hard
                scrypt → memory-hard but less flexible
                ```
                
                Argon2 solves:
                
                ```
                ✔ CPU hardness
                ✔ memory hardness
                ✔ parallelism control
                ```
                
            - types
                
                # 🧩 Types of Argon2
                
                There are 3 variants:
                
                | Type | Use |
                | --- | --- |
                | Argon2d | GPU-resistant (not safe vs side-channel) |
                | Argon2i | side-channel safe |
                | Argon2id | ✅ best of both (recommended) |
            - overal
                
                # ⚙️ Core parameters
                
                Argon2 is powerful because you control **3 dimensions**:
                
                ---
                
                ## 1️⃣ Memory cost
                
                ```
                memoryCost = how much RAM to use
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                64 MB, 128 MB, 256 MB
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 2️⃣ Time cost
                
                ```
                timeCost = how many iterations
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                3, 4, 5
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 3️⃣ Parallelism
                
                ```
                parallelism = number of threads
                ```
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                1–4 threads
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 Compared to scrypt
                
                | Feature | scrypt | Argon2 |
                | --- | --- | --- |
                | Memory control | indirect | direct |
                | CPU control | indirect | direct |
                | Parallelism | limited | full control |
                | Security | good | best |
                
                ---
                
                # 🔐 Hash format
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$Wm9uZVNlY3VyZVNhbHQ$hashvalue...
                ```
                
                Breakdown:
                
                ```
                argon2id → type
                m=65536 → memory (64MB)
                t=3     → iterations
                p=4     → threads
                salt    → encoded salt
                hash    → result
                ```
                
                👉 Like bcrypt, everything is stored **in one string**
                
                ---
                
                # 🧪 Node.js example
                
                Install:
                
                ```
                npm i argon2
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Hash password
                
                ```
                constargon2=require("argon2");
                
                asyncfunctionhashPassword(password) {
                consthash=awaitargon2.hash(password, {
                    type:argon2.argon2id,
                    memoryCost:2**16,// 65536 KB = 64 MB
                    timeCost:3,
                    parallelism:1,
                  });
                
                returnhash;
                }
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Verify password
                
                ```
                asyncfunctionverifyPassword(hash,password) {
                returnawaitargon2.verify(hash,password);
                }
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Full demo
                
                ```
                constargon2=require("argon2");
                
                asyncfunctionrun() {
                constpassword="123456";
                
                consthash=awaitargon2.hash(password);
                
                console.log("Hash:",hash);
                
                constcorrect=awaitargon2.verify(hash,"123456");
                constwrong=awaitargon2.verify(hash,"wrong");
                
                console.log("Correct:",correct);
                console.log("Wrong:",wrong);
                }
                
                run();
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 Why Argon2 is strong
                
                ## 1. Memory-hard
                
                ```
                forces RAM usage → kills GPU advantage
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 2. Time-hard
                
                ```
                multiple iterations → slows brute-force
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 3. Parallelism control
                
                ```
                hard to optimize on hardware
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 4. Everything stored in hash
                
                ```
                ✔ salt
                ✔ memory
                ✔ time
                ✔ threads
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 Real backend flow
                
                ## Register
                
                ```
                password → argon2.hash() → store hash
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Login
                
                ```
                input → argon2.verify(hash)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚠️ Best practice config
                
                ```
                argon2.hash(password, {
                  type:argon2.argon2id,
                  memoryCost:65536,// 64MB
                  timeCost:3,
                  parallelism:1,
                });
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 💡 Interview answer
                
                > Argon2 is a modern password hashing algorithm that provides resistance against brute-force attacks by combining memory hardness, CPU cost, and parallelism. It supports different variants, with Argon2id being the recommended choice for general password hashing.
                > 
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 Final mental model
                
                ```
                bcrypt → CPU only
                scrypt → CPU + memory
                argon2 → CPU + memory + threads (best)
                ```
                
            - side channel
                
                # 🧠 What is a *side-channel*?
                
                👉 A **side-channel** is:
                
                ```
                Getting secret information NOT from the algorithm itself,
                but from how it behaves while running
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🔍 In simple words
                
                Instead of breaking the hash directly, attacker observes:
                
                ```
                ✔ time taken
                ✔ memory usage
                ✔ CPU usage
                ✔ power consumption (advanced)
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚡ Example (timing attack)
                
                Imagine login code:
                
                ```
                if (inputPassword===realPassword) {
                returntrue;
                }
                ```
                
                👉 This compares character by character.
                
                So attacker can measure:
                
                ```
                "p"        → fails fast
                "pa"       → slightly slower
                "pas"      → slower
                "pass..."  → even slower
                ```
                
                👉 They guess password **one char at a time** using time differences.
                
                ---
                
                # 🔐 In hashing context (Argon2)
                
                Now apply this to Argon2.
                
                ## Problem
                
                Some algorithms access memory like this:
                
                ```
                index = derived_from_secret_data
                memory[index]
                ```
                
                👉 If attacker can observe:
                
                ```
                which memory locations are accessed
                ```
                
                They may infer:
                
                ```
                something about the password
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧩 Argon2 variants and side-channel
                
                ## Argon2d
                
                ```
                Memory access depends on password ❌
                ```
                
                👉 Faster, GPU-resistant
                
                👉 BUT vulnerable to side-channel attacks
                
                ---
                
                ## Argon2i
                
                ```
                Memory access independent of password ✅
                ```
                
                👉 Safe against side-channel
                
                👉 Slightly weaker against GPU attacks
                
                ---
                
                ## Argon2id (recommended)
                
                ```
                Mix of both ✅
                ```
                
                👉 First part → safe (Argon2i style)
                
                👉 Later part → strong (Argon2d style)
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 Why side-channel matters
                
                In real world:
                
                ```
                Cloud servers
                Shared hardware
                Virtual machines
                ```
                
                Attackers can:
                
                ```
                ✔ measure timing differences
                ✔ observe cache behavior
                ✔ exploit CPU cache leaks
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # ⚡ Real-world example
                
                Attackers can:
                
                ```
                Measure response time differences
                → deduce internal behavior
                → recover secret bits
                ```
                
                This has happened in:
                
                - TLS attacks
                - CPU cache attacks
                - Spectre/Meltdown class attacks
                
                ---
                
                # 🔥 Simple analogy
                
                ```
                Normal attack:
                Try to open safe directly 🔐
                
                Side-channel:
                Listen to clicks while turning dial 🔊
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🧠 In one sentence
                
                > A side-channel attack extracts sensitive information by observing how a system behaves (like timing or memory access), rather than directly breaking the cryptographic algorithm.
                > 
                
                ---
                
                # 💡 Why Argon2id is best
                
                ```
                Argon2d → strong but leaks patterns
                Argon2i → safe but slightly weaker
                Argon2id → balanced ✅
                ```
                
                ---
                
                # 🚀 Final mental model
                
                ```
                Algorithm security = math
                Side-channel security = implementation behavior
                ```
                
        - monolith vs microservices
            
            # 🧠 Core idea
            
            ```
            Monolith = one big application
            Microservices = many small independent services
            ```
            
            But that definition is too shallow. Let’s go deeper.
            
            ---
            
            # 🏗️ 1. Architecture (REAL difference)
            
            ## 🟢 Monolith
            
            ```
            Frontend → Backend (one app) → DB
            ```
            
            Everything lives together:
            
            - auth
            - payments
            - users
            - products
            
            👉 Same codebase, same deployment
            
            ---
            
            ## 🔵 Microservices
            
            ```
            Frontend → API Gateway
                          ↓
                 ┌────────┼────────┐
               Auth     Users    Orders
                 ↓         ↓         ↓
               DB        DB        DB
            ```
            
            👉 Each service:
            
            - separate codebase
            - separate DB
            - separate deployment
            
            ---
            
            # ⚙️ 2. Code organization
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Single repo
            Single runtime
            Shared memory
            ```
            
            Example:
            
            ```
            /controllers
            /services
            /models
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Multiple repos or modules
            Each service = standalone app
            ```
            
            Example:
            
            ```
            auth-service/
            user-service/
            order-service/
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🚀 3. Deployment
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Change one line → redeploy whole app
            ```
            
            Risk:
            
            ```
            ✔ simple
            ❌ affects everything
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Change auth → deploy auth only
            ```
            
            Risk:
            
            ```
            ✔ isolated deployments
            ❌ coordination complexity
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🔥 4. Scaling (VERY IMPORTANT)
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Scale entire app
            ```
            
            ```
            More users → scale whole server
            ```
            
            Problem:
            
            ```
            Orders heavy → but you scale everything (waste)
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Scale only needed service
            ```
            
            Example:
            
            ```
            Orders service → 10 instances
            Auth service → 2 instances
            ```
            
            👉 Efficient scaling
            
            ---
            
            # 🧠 5. Database design
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Single database
            ```
            
            ```
            ✔ easy joins
            ✔ strong consistency
            ❌ tight coupling
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Database per service
            ```
            
            ```
            ✔ isolation
            ✔ independent scaling
            ❌ no joins
            ❌ eventual consistency
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # ⚠️ 6. Data consistency
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            ACID transactions
            ```
            
            Example:
            
            ```
            BEGIN;
            UPDATE users;
            UPDATE orders;
            COMMIT;
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Distributed transactions ❌
            ```
            
            Instead:
            
            ```
            ✔ eventual consistency
            ✔ Saga pattern
            ✔ message queues
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 📡 7. Communication
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Function calls (in-memory)
            ```
            
            ```
            userService.createUser()
            ```
            
            👉 Fast
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Network calls
            ```
            
            ```
            HTTP / gRPC / Kafka / RabbitMQ
            ```
            
            👉 Slower + failure-prone
            
            ---
            
            # 🔥 8. Failure handling
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            One failure → whole app affected
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            One service fails → others still run
            ```
            
            BUT:
            
            ```
            ✔ need circuit breakers
            ✔ need retries
            ✔ need timeouts
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🧠 9. Complexity (this is where people fail interviews)
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            ✔ simple to build
            ✔ simple to debug
            ❌ becomes messy at scale
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            ✔ scalable
            ✔ flexible
            ❌ distributed system complexity
            ❌ debugging nightmare
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 📊 10. Performance
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            ✔ faster (no network calls)
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            ❌ slower (network latency)
            ✔ can scale horizontally
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🔐 11. Security
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            ✔ single security boundary
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            ✔ multiple services → multiple attack points
            ✔ need auth between services (JWT, mTLS)
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 👥 12. Team scaling
            
            ## Monolith
            
            ```
            Small team → perfect
            Large team → conflicts
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Microservices
            
            ```
            Teams own services
            Independent development
            ```
            
            Example:
            
            ```
            Team A → Auth
            Team B → Orders
            Team C → Payments
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 💣 13. Real-world problems (IMPORTANT)
            
            ## Microservices introduce:
            
            ```
            ✔ network failures
            ✔ partial failures
            ✔ data inconsistency
            ✔ distributed debugging
            ✔ observability needs
            ```
            
            So you need:
            
            ```
            ✔ logging (ELK)
            ✔ tracing (Jaeger)
            ✔ monitoring (Prometheus)
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🧠 14. When to use what
            
            ## Use Monolith when:
            
            ```
            ✔ startup
            ✔ small team
            ✔ fast development needed
            ✔ simple system
            ```
            
            ---
            
            ## Use Microservices when:
            
            ```
            ✔ large system
            ✔ high scalability needed
            ✔ multiple teams
            ✔ complex domain
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # ⚡ 15. Hybrid approach (REAL WORLD)
            
            Most companies do:
            
            ```
            Modular Monolith → Microservices later
            ```
            
            👉 Start:
            
            ```
            single app with clean modules
            ```
            
            👉 Then split:
            
            ```
            extract services gradually
            ```
            
            ---
            
            # 🧠 Interview-level answer
            
            If asked:
            
            > “Monolith vs Microservices?”
            > 
            
            You say:
            
            > A monolith is a single unified application with shared code and database, making it simpler to develop and deploy but harder to scale and maintain at large scale. Microservices split the system into independent services, each with its own logic and database, enabling independent scaling and deployment but introducing complexity such as network communication, distributed data consistency, and operational overhead.
            > 
            
            ---
            
            # 🔥 Final mental model
            
            ```
            Monolith = simplicity
            Microservices = scalability + complexity
            ```

            - ⚙️ How Docker actually works (under the hood)
                
                Docker uses **OS-level virtualization**, not full VMs.
                
                ### 🔥 Key components:
                
                ### 1. **Kernel sharing**
                
                - All containers share **host OS kernel**
                - No full OS per container
                
                👉 This is why Docker is:
                
                - ⚡ fast
                - 🪶 lightweight
                
                ---
                
                ### 2. **Namespaces (isolation)**
                
                Each container has isolated:
                
                - Process list (PID)
                - Network
                - Filesystem
                - Users
                
                👉 Container thinks:
                
                > “I am the only system”
                > 
                
                ---
                
                ### 3. **cgroups (resource control)**
                
                Limit:
                
                - CPU
                - RAM
                - Disk I/O
                
                ---
                
                ### 4. **Union File System (layers)**
                
                Images are built in layers:
                
                ```
                Ubuntu → Node → App → Code
                ```
                
                👉 Benefits:
                
                - caching
                - reuse
                - fast builds
            - 📦 Docker Architecture
                
                ```
                Docker CLI → Docker Daemon → Containers
                ```
                
                ### Components:
                
                - **Docker Client** → CLI (`docker build`, `docker run`)
                - **Docker Daemon** → does the work
                - **Images** → templates
                - **Containers** → running instances
            - 🧩 Key Concepts (must know)
                
                ## 1. Image
                
                > Blueprint of your app
                > 
                
                Example:
                
                ```
                node:18
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## 2. Container
                
                > Running instance of image
                > 
                
                ---
                
                ## 3. Dockerfile
                
                > Instructions to build image
                > 
                
                ---
                
                ## 4. Volume
                
                > Persistent storage
                > 
                
                ---
                
                ## 5. Network
                
                > Communication between containers
                > 
            - Ecample Dockerfile
                
                ```jsx
                FROM node:18
                
                WORKDIR /app
                
                COPY package*.json ./
                RUN npm install
                
                COPY . .
                
                EXPOSE 3000
                
                CMD ["npm", "run", "start"]

                ## Build
                
                ```
                docker build-t my-app .
                ```
                
                ---
                
                ## Run
                
                ```

                ```
                
            - DOCKER VS VM
                
                
                | Feature | Docker | VM |
                | --- | --- | --- |
                | OS | Shared | Separate |
                | Startup | ms | minutes |
                | Size | MB | GB |
                | Isolation | Process-level | Full OS |
                | Performance | Near native | slower |

                - What is container
                    - 🧠 1. What is a Docker Container (REAL definition)
                        
                        A **running instance of an image** with **process isolation + filesystem isolation + network isolation + resource limits**
                        
                        ## 🔥 Important correction
                        
                        Container ≠ VM
                        
                        Container = **just a process (or processes)** with isolation
                        
                    - ⚙️ 2. What happens when you run a container
                        
                        ```
                        docker run my-app
                        ```
                        
                        👉 Internally:
                        
                        ### Step-by-step:
                        
                        1. Pull image (if not exists)
                        2. Create container metadata
                        3. Create writable layer
                        4. Setup namespaces
                        5. Setup cgroups
                        6. Setup network
                        7. Start main process
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🧠 Final result
                        
                        ```
                        Isolated process + isolated FS + isolated network
                        ```
                        
                    - 🧩 3. Core building blocks (VERY IMPORTANT)
                        
                        ## 1. Namespaces (isolation)
                        
                        Linux feature → isolates resources
                        
                        Types:
                        
                        | Namespace | What it isolates |
                        | --- | --- |
                        | PID | processes |
                        | NET | network |
                        | MNT | filesystem |
                        | UTS | hostname |
                        | IPC | inter-process comm |
                        | USER | users |
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ### 🔥 Example
                        
                        Inside container:
                        
                        ```
                        ps aux
                        ```
                        
                        👉 You only see container processes
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 2. cgroups (resource limits)
                        
                        Controls:
                        
                        - CPU
                        - RAM
                        - Disk I/O
                        
                        Example:
                        
                        ```
                        docker run--memory=512m--cpus=1 my-app
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 3. OverlayFS (filesystem)
                        
                        From image:
                        
                        ```
                        read-only layers
                        ```
                        
                        Container adds:
                        
                        ```
                        writable layer
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 4. Container = Process (CRITICAL)
                        
                        👉 Inside container:
                        
                        ```
                        CMD ["node","app.js"]
                        ```
                        
                        This becomes:
                        
                        ```
                        PID 1 = node app.js
                        ```

                        ## ⚠️ Important behavior
                        
                        If process dies:
                        
                        👉 container stops
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Interview trap

                        > 
                        
                        Technically yes ❌
                        
                        Practically NO (bad practice)

                        Each container has:

                        - logs

                        | Feature | Container | VM |

                        # 🧠 Interview-level answer
                        
                        > “A Docker container is an isolated process created from an image, using Linux namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource control, and overlay filesystem for storage.”
                        > 
                    
                - what is image
                    - docs
                        
                        
                        > An **immutable, read-only, layered filesystem + metadata** used to create containers.
                        > 
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Key properties
                        
                        - ❌ Not a running thing
                        - ✅ Template / blueprint
                        - ❌ Cannot be changed
                        - ✅ Built once, reused many times
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧩 2. What exactly is inside an Image?
                        
                        An image contains:
                        
                        ### 1. Filesystem (layers)
                        
                        - OS files (e.g. Linux)
                        - libraries
                        - your app code
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ### 2. Metadata (VERY IMPORTANT)
                        
                        Stored as JSON:
                        
                        - default command (CMD)
                        - entrypoint
                        - environment variables
                        - exposed ports
                        - working directory
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Example mentally
                        
                        Image =
                        
                        ```
                        {
                          filesystem: [layer1, layer2, layer3],
                          config: {
                            CMD: ["npm", "start"],
                            WORKDIR: "/app",
                            ENV: {...}
                          }
                        }
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 3. How Image is built (REAL process)
                        
                        When you run:
                        
                        ```
                        docker build-t my-app .
                        ```
                        
                        👉 Docker:
                        
                        ### Step 1 — Read Dockerfile
                        
                        ### Step 2 — Execute line by line
                        
                        ### Step 3 — After each step → create new layer
                        
                        ### Step 4 — Store layers
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Important rule
                        
                        👉 **Each instruction = one layer**
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧩 4. Layer system (MOST IMPORTANT PART)
                        
                        Example:
                        
                        ```
                        FROM node:18
                        WORKDIR /app
                        COPY package.json .
                        RUN npm install
                        COPY . .
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## Result:
                        
                        ```
                        Layer 1 → base OS (node:18)
                        Layer 2 → WORKDIR
                        Layer 3 → package.json
                        Layer 4 → npm install
                        Layer 5 → source code
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## ⚡ Why layers exist
                        
                        ### 1. Reusability
                        
                        Multiple images reuse same base layer
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ### 2. Caching
                        
                        If nothing changed:
                        
                        👉 Docker skips rebuilding that layer
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ### 3. Efficiency
                        
                        Only changed layers are rebuilt/pulled
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # ⚠️ VERY IMPORTANT (interview trap)
                        
                        Order matters:
                        
                        ```
                        COPY . .
                        RUN npm install
                        ```
                        
                        ❌ BAD → every code change reinstall dependencies
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ✔ GOOD:
                        
                        ```
                        COPY package.json .
                        RUN npm install
                        COPY . .
                        ```
                        
                        ---

                        ## 🔹 Locally
                        
                        Stored in:
                        
                        ```
                        /var/lib/docker/
                        ```
                        
                        👉 Internally:
                        
                        - layers stored separately
                        - managed by Docker (you don’t touch)
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔹 Remotely (Registry)
                        
                        Examples:
                        
                        - Docker Hub
                        - AWS ECR
                        - GitHub Container Registry
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Flow
                        
                        ```
                        build → tag → push → pull → run
                        ```
                        
                        # 🧠 6. Image immutability
                        
                        👉 Once built:
                        
                        - cannot be modified
                        - only create new image
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## Why important?
                        
                        - reproducibility
                        - versioning
                        - safe deployments
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 7. Image vs Container (CRITICAL)
                        
                        | Image | Container |
                        | --- | --- |
                        | static | running |
                        | read-only | read-write |
                        | template | instance |
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 🔥 Key relation
                        
                        ```
                        1 Image → many Containers
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 8. Image size (deep insight)
                        
                        Image size = sum of all layers
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## ⚠️ Problem
                        
                        Bad Dockerfile:
                        
                        - huge images
                        - slow deployment

                        ### Use smaller base:
                        
                        ```

                        ```

                        ```
                        
                        👉 Final image = smaller
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 9. Image caching mechanism (VERY IMPORTANT)
                        
                        Docker checks:
                        
                        - instruction
                        - file hash
                        
                        If unchanged:
                        
                        👉 reuse layer
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## Example
                        
                        If only source code changed:
                        
                        👉 Only last layer rebuilds
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 10. Image tagging
                        
                        ```

                        ```

                        ```

                        ---
                        
                        ## ⚠️ Important
                        
                        `latest` ≠ newest always
                        
                        👉 just a label
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 11. Image pull process
                        
                        ```

                        ```
                        
                        👉 Docker:
                        
                        1. Checks local cache
                        2. Downloads missing layers only
                        3. Reuses existing layers
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 12. Image layering deep concept (UNION FS)
                        
                        Docker uses:
                        
                        > Union File System
                        > 
                        
                        👉 combines layers into one view
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## Example
                        
                        ```
                        Layer 1: file A
                        Layer 2: modify file A
                        ```
                        
                        👉 final:
                        
                        - only latest version visible
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 13. How delete works (IMPORTANT)
                        
                        If you delete file:
                        
                        👉 It’s not removed physically
                        
                        👉 Just marked as deleted in upper layer
                        
                        ---
                        
                        # 🧠 14. Image security
                        
                        Images can contain:
                        
                        - vulnerabilities
                        - outdated packages
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## Best practices:
                        
                        - use official images
                        - scan images
                        - keep small

                        # 🔥 FINAL SENIOR-LEVEL UNDERSTANDING
                        
                        > A Docker image is a layered, immutable filesystem snapshot with execution metadata, built through incremental steps and optimized via caching and reuse.
                        > 
                    - image layers
                        
                        Docker stores image/container filesystem data under:
                        
                        ```
                        /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
                        ```
                        
                        With `overlay2`, Docker uses Linux OverlayFS. It combines many read-only image layers with one writable container layer using these ideas:
                        
                        ```
                        lowerdir  = read-only image layers
                        upperdir  = container writable layer
                        merged    = final visible filesystem
                        workdir   = internal OverlayFS work directory
                        ```
                        
                        So when container runs:
                        
                        ```
                        Image layer 1  \
                        Image layer 2   > lowerdir
                        Image layer 3  /
                        Container writes → upperdir
                        Visible container FS → merged
                        ```
                        
                        Docker docs say storage drivers manage both image layers and the writable container layer, using stackable layers and copy-on-write. `overlay2` supports up to 128 lower OverlayFS layers.
                        
                        Important: **never manually delete `/var/lib/docker/overlay2` files**. Use Docker commands like:
                        
                        ```
                        docker system prune
                        docker image prune
                        docker container prune
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 2. How image hashing works
                        
                        Docker/OCI images are **content-addressable**.
                        
                        Meaning: Docker does not identify image content mainly by name. It identifies real content by cryptographic hashes, usually:
                        
                        ```
                        sha256:<hash>
                        ```
                        
                        An image is built from:
                        
                        ```
                        manifest + config JSON + layer blobs
                        ```
                        
                        The OCI spec says image manifests support content-addressable images by hashing image config and components. Docker image digests are immutable SHA-256 identifiers representing image content.
                        
                        So:
                        
                        ```
                        node:18
                        ```
                        
                        is a **tag**.
                        
                        But:
                        
                        ```
                        node@sha256:abc...
                        ```
                        
                        is an exact immutable image version.
                        
                        Interview point:
                        
                        > Tags can change. Digests do not change unless content changes.
                        > 
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 3. How Docker deduplicates layers
                        
                        Docker deduplicates by **layer digest**.
                        
                        Example:
                        
                        ```
                        Image A:
                        ubuntu layer
                        node layer
                        app A layer
                        
                        Image B:
                        ubuntu layer
                        node layer
                        app B layer
                        ```
                        
                        Docker stores shared layers only once:
                        
                        ```
                        ubuntu layer → stored once
                        node layer   → stored once
                        app layers   → separate
                        ```
                        
                        That is why pulling multiple Node images is faster after the first one.
                        
                        Also, during build, Docker reuses cached layers when the instruction and files it depends on have not changed. For `COPY` and `ADD`, Docker calculates checksums from file metadata; file modification time alone does not invalidate cache.
                        
                        Simple rule:
                        
                        ```
                        same content → same digest → reused
                        different content → different digest → new layer
                        ```
                        
                        ---
                        
                        ## 4. Perfect production Dockerfile for NestJS
                        
                        Use multi-stage build: one stage installs/builds, final stage only runs production output. Docker recommends multi-stage builds because they separate build environment from runtime and reduce final image size/attack surface.
                        
                        ```
                        # ---------- Stage 1: dependencies ----------
                        FROM node:22-alpineAS deps
                        
                        WORKDIR /app
                        
                        COPY package*.json ./
                        
                        RUN npm ci
                        
                        # ---------- Stage 2: build ----------
                        FROM node:22-alpineAS builder
                        
                        WORKDIR /app
                        
                        COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
                        COPY . .
                        
                        RUN npm run build
                        
                        # ---------- Stage 3: production ----------
                        FROM node:22-alpineAS production
                        
                        WORKDIR /app
                        
                        ENV NODE_ENV=production
                        
                        COPY package*.json ./
                        
                        RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force
                        
                        COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
                        
                        EXPOSE3000
                        
                        USER node
                        
                        CMD ["node","dist/main.js"]
                        ```
                        
                        Add `.dockerignore`:
                        
                        ```
                        node_modules
                        dist
                        .git
                        .env
                        npm-debug.log
                        Dockerfile
                        docker-compose.yml
                        ```
                        
                        Interview-level summary:
                        
                        > Docker images are immutable, content-addressed layered filesystems. `overlay2` mounts read-only image layers as `lowerdir`, adds a writable `upperdir` for the container, and exposes the final filesystem through `merged`. Docker deduplicates layers by digest, so identical layers ar

                - what is docker daemon
                    
                    # 🧠 1. What is Docker Daemon (real definition)
                    
                    Docker Daemon is:
                    
                    > A **background service (server)** that manages **images, containers, networks, and volumes**
                    > 
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 Simple mental model
                    
                    ```
                    Docker CLI → Docker Daemon → OS (kernel)
                    ```
                    
                    👉 You never talk to Docker directly
                    
                    👉 You always talk to **dockerd**
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # ⚙️ 2. What happens when you run a command
                    
                    Example:
                    
                    ```
                    docker run my-app
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Step-by-step (REAL FLOW)
                    
                    1. CLI sends request to daemon (via API)
                    2. Daemon:
                        - checks image
                        - pulls if needed
                    3. Creates container
                    4. Configures:
                        - filesystem
                        - networking
                        - cgroups
                    5. Starts process
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 Important
                    
                    👉 CLI = just a client
                    
                    👉 Daemon = does everything
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧩 3. Communication (VERY IMPORTANT)
                    
                    CLI communicates with daemon via:
                    
                    ### 🔹 Unix socket (default)
                    
                    ```
                    /var/run/docker.sock
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 🔹 Or TCP (remote Docker)
                    
                    ```
                    tcp://host:2375
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## ⚠️ Security insight
                    
                    If someone accesses:
                    
                    ```
                    /var/run/docker.sock
                    ```
                    
                    👉 They can control your entire system ❗
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 4. What daemon manages
                    
                    Daemon handles:
                    
                    ### 1. Images
                    
                    - build
                    - pull
                    - push
                    - delete
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 2. Containers
                    
                    - create
                    - start
                    - stop
                    - remove
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 3. Networks
                    
                    - bridge
                    - host
                    - overlay
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 4. Volumes
                    
                    - persistent storage
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 5. Daemon architecture (deep)
                    
                    Docker daemon uses:
                    
                    - container runtime (containerd)
                    - low-level runtime (runc)
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 Flow:
                    
                    ```
                    dockerd → containerd → runc → kernel
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Explanation:
                    
                    - **dockerd** → high-level manager
                    - **containerd** → container lifecycle manager
                    - **runc** → creates container (namespaces + cgroups)
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## ⚡ Key insight
                    
                    👉 Docker itself does NOT create containers directly
                    
                    👉 It delegates to runtimes
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 6. containerd (important)
                    
                    containerd
                    
                    - manages containers lifecycle
                    - handles image pulling
                    - manages storage
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 7. runc (low-level)
                    
                    - creates container using Linux features:
                        - namespaces
                        - cgroups
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 8. Daemon responsibilities (detailed)
                    
                    When creating container:
                    
                    Daemon:
                    
                    1. Pulls image
                    2. Extracts layers
                    3. Mounts filesystem (overlay2)
                    4. Sets namespaces
                    5. Sets cgroups
                    6. Configures network
                    7. Calls runc
                    8. Starts process
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 9. Daemon configuration
                    
                    File:
                    
                    ```
                    /etc/docker/daemon.json
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Example:
                    
                    ```
                    {
                      "log-driver":"json-file",
                      "storage-driver":"overlay2",
                      "registry-mirrors": ["https://mirror.gcr.io"]
                    }
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 10. Logs & debugging
                    
                    Check daemon logs:
                    
                    ```
                    journalctl-u docker
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 11. Daemon lifecycle
                    
                    Start:
                    
                    ```
                    systemctlstart docker
                    ```
                    
                    Stop:
                    
                    ```
                    systemctlstop docker
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## ⚠️ Important
                    
                    If daemon stops:
                    
                    👉 ALL containers stop
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 12. Root vs rootless mode
                    
                    ### Root mode (default)
                    
                    - full system access
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Rootless mode
                    
                    - runs without root privileges
                    - more secure
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 13. Performance considerations
                    
                    Daemon handles:
                    
                    - many containers
                    - image caching
                    - networking
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## ⚠️ Bottleneck
                    
                    If daemon overloaded:
                    
                    - slow container startup
                    - delays in builds
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 14. Security risks (VERY IMPORTANT)
                    
                    ### 1. Docker socket exposure
                    
                    ```
                    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
                    ```
                    
                    👉 Dangerous ❗
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### 2. Root privileges
                    
                    Containers can escalate if misconfigured
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 15. Real-world mapping (your case)
                    
                    You:
                    
                    - deploy Node apps
                    - use PM2
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## With Docker:
                    
                    Daemon replaces:
                    
                    - process manager
                    - environment manager
                    - deployment logic
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🔥 CRITICAL INSIGHT
                    
                    > Docker daemon is the **brain of Docker**, orchestrating container lifecycle and delegating execution to lower-level runtimes.
                    > 
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 Interview-level answer
                    
                    > “Docker daemon is the background service that manages Docker objects and communicates with the CLI via API, delegating container execution to containerd and runc while configuring namespaces, cgroups, networking, and storage.”
                    > 
                - how docker lives in OS
                    
                    # 🧠 1. Where Docker “lives” in the OS
                    
                    Docker is **not part of the kernel**.
                    
                    👉 It lives as:
                    
                    ```
                    User space application (process)
                    ```
                    
                    Main process:
                    
                    - dockerd
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 So structure is:
                    
                    ```
                    [ Your commands (CLI) ]
                            ↓
                    [ dockerd (user space process) ]
                            ↓
                    [ containerd → runc ]
                            ↓
                    [ Linux Kernel ]
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # ⚙️ 2. What parts belong where
                    
                    ## 🔹 User space (Docker lives here)
                    
                    - docker CLI
                    - dockerd
                    - containerd
                    - runc
                    
                    👉 These are just **normal Linux processes**
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔹 Kernel space (real magic happens here)
                    
                    Docker uses kernel features:
                    
                    - namespaces → isolation
                    - cgroups → resource limits
                    - overlayfs → filesystem layers
                    - networking stack → virtual networks
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 Key insight
                    
                    > Docker itself does NOT create containers
                    > 
                    > 
                    > Linux kernel does
                    > 
                    
                    Docker just:
                    
                    👉 **tells kernel what to do**
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 3. What happens when Docker runs
                    
                    You type:
                    
                    ```
                    docker run nginx
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Internally:
                    
                    ### Step 1
                    
                    CLI → sends request to dockerd
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Step 2
                    
                    dockerd → calls containerd
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Step 3
                    
                    containerd → calls runc
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Step 4
                    
                    runc → asks kernel:
                    
                    - create namespaces
                    - assign cgroups
                    - mount filesystem
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ### Step 5
                    
                    Kernel creates isolated process
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Result:
                    
                    ```
                    Container = kernel-isolated process
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧩 4. How Docker appears in OS (practically)
                    
                    Run:
                    
                    ```
                    ps aux |grep docker
                    ```
                    
                    You’ll see:
                    
                    - dockerd
                    - containerd
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Run:
                    
                    ```
                    ps aux inside container
                    ```
                    
                    👉 You’ll see your app
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## 🔥 Important
                    
                    Containers are visible in host:
                    
                    ```
                    ps aux
                    ```
                    
                    👉 Just processes!
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 5. Filesystem presence
                    
                    Docker stores data in:
                    
                    ```
                    /var/lib/docker/
                    ```
                    
                    Inside:
                    
                    - images (layers)
                    - containers
                    - volumes
                    - networks
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Overlay2 example:
                    
                    ```
                    /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 6. Networking in OS
                    
                    Docker creates:
                    
                    - virtual interfaces (veth)
                    - bridges (`docker0`)
                    - iptables rules
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Example:
                    
                    ```
                    ip a
                    ```
                    
                    You’ll see:
                    
                    ```
                    docker0
                    vethXXXXX
                    ```
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 7. Resource control in OS
                    
                    Docker uses:
                    
                    ```
                    /sys/fs/cgroup/
                    ```
                    
                    👉 Kernel enforces:
                    
                    - memory limits
                    - CPU limits
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 8. Is Docker a VM?
                    
                    ❌ NO
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Why?
                    
                    | Feature | Docker |
                    | --- | --- |
                    | Kernel | shared |
                    | Process | real OS process |
                    | Isolation | kernel-based |
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 9. How Docker starts
                    
                    ```
                    systemctlstart docker
                    ```
                    
                    👉 Starts:
                    
                    - dockerd
                    - containerd
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## ⚠️ If dockerd dies
                    
                    👉 all containers stop
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 10. Windows / Mac case (IMPORTANT)
                    
                    Linux:
                    
                    👉 Docker runs directly
                    
                    ---
                    
                    Windows / Mac:
                    
                    👉 Docker runs inside VM
                    
                    ---
                    
                    ## Why?
                    
                    Because:
                    
                    - Docker needs Linux kernel
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🔥 FINAL INSIGHT (VERY IMPORTANT)
                    
                    > Docker is just a user-space tool that orchestrates Linux kernel features to create isolated processes called containers.
                    > 
                    
                    ---
                    
                    # 🧠 Interview-level answer
                    
                    > “Docker runs as a user-space daemon (dockerd) that communicates with the Linux kernel to create isolated processes using namespaces, cgroups, and overlay filesystems. Containers are not virtual machines but kernel-isolated processes.”
                    >
